primaryText.ACT:25:11: For if I have done wrong and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
primaryText.ACT:25:12: Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”
primaryText.ACT:25:7: When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing against him many and grievous charges which they could not prove,
primaryText.ACT:25:8: while he said in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.”
primaryText.ACT:25:9: But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged by me there concerning these things?”

evidence.quote: 7. the Jews ... from Jerusalem--clamorously, as at Jerusalem; see Ac 25:24.
9-10. Festus, willing to do the Jews a pleasure--to ingratiate himself with them.

11. I appeal to Cæsar--The right of appeal to the supreme power, in case of life and death, was secured by an ancient law to every Roman citizen, and continued under the empire. Had Festus shown any disposition to pronounce final judgment, Paul, strong in the consciousness of his innocence and the justice of a Roman tribunal, would not ha
12. Festus--little expecting such an appeal, but bound to respect it.

primaryText.ACT:25:13: Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus.
primaryText.ACT:25:14: As he stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a certain man left a prisoner by Felix;
primaryText.ACT:25:15: about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, asking for a sentence against him.
primaryText.ACT:25:16: I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him.
primaryText.ACT:25:17: When therefore they had come together here, I didn’t delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat and commanded the man to be brought.

evidence.quote: 13. King Agrippa--great-grandson of Herod the Great, and Drusilla's brother (see on Ac 24:24). On his father's awful death (Ac 12:23), being thought too young (seventeen) to succeed, Judea, was attached to the province of Syria. Four years after, on the death of his uncle Herod, he was made king of the northern principalities of Chalcis,
14-15. when there many--"several"
16-21. to deliver any man to die--On the word "deliver up," see on Ac 25:11.

primaryText.ACT:25:18: When the accusers stood up, they brought no charges against him of such things as I supposed;
primaryText.ACT:25:19: but had certain questions against him about their own religion and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
primaryText.ACT:25:20: Being perplexed how to inquire concerning these things, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these matters.
primaryText.ACT:25:21: But when Paul had appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor, I commanded him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar.”

evidence.quote: 16-21. to deliver any man to die--On the word "deliver up," see on Ac 25:11.

primaryText.ACT:25:22: Agrippa said to Festus, “I also would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you shall hear him.”
primaryText.ACT:25:23: So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.
primaryText.ACT:25:24: Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all men who are here present with us, you see this man about whom all the multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
primaryText.ACT:25:25: But when I found that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and as he himself appealed to the emperor, I determined to send him,
primaryText.ACT:25:26: of whom I have no certain thing to write to my lord. Therefore I have brought him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, that, after examination I may have something to write.
primaryText.ACT:25:27: For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.”

evidence.quote: 22-27. I would also hear--"should like to hear."

primaryText.ACT:26:1: Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense.
primaryText.ACT:26:2: “I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I am to make my defense before you today concerning all the things the Jews accuse me of,
primaryText.ACT:26:3: especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently.

evidence.quote: This speech, though in substance the same as that from the fortress stairs of Jerusalem (Ac 22:1-29), differs from it in being less directed to meet the charge of apostasy from the Jewish faith, and giving more enlarged views of his remarkable change and apostolic commission, and the divine support under which he was enabled to brave the

primaryText.ACT:26:4: “Indeed, all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem;
primaryText.ACT:26:5: having known me from the first, if they are willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.

evidence.quote: 4-5. from my youth, which was at the first ... at Jerusalem, know all the Jews; which knew me from the beginning--plainly showing that he received his education, even from early youth, at Jerusalem. See on Ac 22:3.

primaryText.ACT:26:6: Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
primaryText.ACT:26:7: which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa!

evidence.quote: 6-7. I ... am judged for the hope of the promise made ... to our fathers--"for believing that the promise of Messiah, the Hope of the Church (Ac 13:32; 28:20) has been fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth risen from the dead."

primaryText.ACT:26:8: Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead?

evidence.quote: 8. Why should it be thought a thing incredible ... that God should raise the dead?--rather, "Why is it judged a thing incredible if God raises the dead?" the case being viewed as an accomplished fact. No one dared to call in question the overwhelming evidence of the resurrection of Jesus, which proclaimed Him to be the Christ, the Son of

primaryText.ACT:26:10: I also did this in Jerusalem. I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them.
primaryText.ACT:26:11: Punishing them often in all the synagogues, I tried to make them blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities.
primaryText.ACT:26:12: “Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests,
primaryText.ACT:26:13: at noon, O king, I saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who traveled with me.
primaryText.ACT:26:14: When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’
primaryText.ACT:26:15: “I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ “He said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
primaryText.ACT:26:9: “I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.

evidence.quote: 9-15. (See on Ac 9:1, &c.; and compare Ac 22:4, &c.)

primaryText.ACT:26:16: But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen and of the things which I will reveal to you;
primaryText.ACT:26:17: delivering you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you,
primaryText.ACT:26:18: to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’

evidence.quote: 16-18. But rise, &c.--Here the apostle appears to condense into one statement various sayings of his Lord to him in visions at different times, in order to present at one view the grandeur of the commission with which his Master had clothed him [Alford].

primaryText.ACT:26:19: “Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,
primaryText.ACT:26:20: but declared first to them of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
primaryText.ACT:26:21: For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.

evidence.quote: 19-21. Whereupon, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision--This musical and elevated strain, which carries the reader along with it, and doubtless did the hearers, bespeaks the lofty region of thought and feeling to which the apostle had risen while rehearsing his Master's communications to him from heaven.

primaryText.ACT:26:22: Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen,
primaryText.ACT:26:23: how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.”

evidence.quote: 22-23. having obtained help--"succor."

primaryText.ACT:26:24: As he thus made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!”

evidence.quote: 24. Festus said with a loud voice--surprised and bewildered.

primaryText.ACT:26:25: But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness.
primaryText.ACT:26:26: For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner.

evidence.quote: 25-26. I am not mad, most noble Festus, but, &c.--Can anything surpass this reply, for readiness, self-possession, calm dignity? Every word of it refuted the rude charge, though Festus, probably, did not intend to hurt the prisoner's feelings.

primaryText.ACT:26:27: King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
primaryText.ACT:26:28: Agrippa said to Paul, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?”
primaryText.ACT:26:29: Paul said, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.”

evidence.quote: 27-29. believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest--The courage and confidence here shown proceeded from a vivid persuasion of Agrippa's knowledge of the facts and faith in the predictions which they verified; and the king's reply is the highest testimony to the correctness of these presumptions and the immense power of such b

primaryText.ACT:26:30: The king rose up with the governor and Bernice, and those who sat with them.
primaryText.ACT:26:31: When they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.”
primaryText.ACT:26:32: Agrippa said to Festus, “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

evidence.quote: 30-32. when he had thus spoken, the king rose--not over-easy, we may be sure.

primaryText.ACT:27:1: When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band.
primaryText.ACT:27:2: Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia, we put to sea, Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica being with us.
primaryText.ACT:27:3: The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.

evidence.quote: 1. we should sail, &c.--The "we" here reintroduces the historian as one of the company. Not that he had left the apostle from the time when he last included himself (Ac 21:18), but the apostle was parted from him by his arrest and imprisonment, until now, when they met in the ship.
2. a ship of--belonging to.
3. next day we touched at Sidon--To reach this ancient and celebrated Mediterranean port, about seventy miles north from Cæsarea, in one day, they must have had a fair wind.

primaryText.ACT:27:4: Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
primaryText.ACT:27:5: When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.
primaryText.ACT:27:6: There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
primaryText.ACT:27:7: When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.
primaryText.ACT:27:8: With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.

evidence.quote: 4. when we had launched--"set sail."
5. when we had sailed over the Sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia--coasts with which Paul had been long familiar, the one, perhaps, from boyhood, the other from the time of his first missionary tour.

6. there ... found a ship of Alexandria, sailing into Italy, and he put us therein--(See on Ac 27:2). As Egypt was the granary of Italy, and this vessel was laden with wheat (Ac 27:35), we need not wonder it was large enough to carry two hundred seventy-six souls, passengers and crew together (Ac 27:37). Besides, the Egyptian merchantmen,
7. sailed slowly many days--owing to contrary winds.
8. And hardly passing it--"with difficulty coasting along it," from the same cause as before, the westerly current and head winds.

primaryText.ACT:27:10: and said to them, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”
primaryText.ACT:27:11: But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul.
primaryText.ACT:27:12: Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking southwest and northwest.
primaryText.ACT:27:9: When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them

evidence.quote: 9-10. when much time was spent--since leaving Cæsarea. But for unforeseen delays they might have reached the Italian coast before the stormy season.

11. Nevertheless the centurion believed the master and owner ... more than ... Paul--He would naturally think them best able to judge, and there was much to say for their opinion, as the bay at Fair Havens, being open to nearly one-half of the compass, could not be a good winter harbor.
12. Phenice--"Phenix," now called Lutro.

primaryText.ACT:27:13: When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore.
primaryText.ACT:27:14: But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon.
primaryText.ACT:27:15: When the ship was caught and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.
primaryText.ACT:27:16: Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat.
primaryText.ACT:27:17: After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along.
primaryText.ACT:27:18: As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard.
primaryText.ACT:27:19: On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.
primaryText.ACT:27:20: When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.

evidence.quote: 13. when the south wind blew softly, supposing they had attained their purpose--With such a wind they had every prospect of reaching their destination in a few hours.
14-15. a tempestuous--"typhonic"
island ... Clauda--southwest of Crete, now called Gonzo; about twenty-three miles to leeward.
19-20. cast out with our own hands--passengers and crew together.

primaryText.ACT:27:21: When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them and said, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete and have gotten this injury and loss.
primaryText.ACT:27:22: Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
primaryText.ACT:27:23: For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve,
primaryText.ACT:27:24: saying, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’
primaryText.ACT:27:25: Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.
primaryText.ACT:27:26: But we must run aground on a certain island.”

evidence.quote: 21-26. But after long abstinence--(See on Ac 27:33). "The hardships which the crew endured during a gale of such continuance, and their exhaustion from laboring at the pumps and hunger, may be imagined, but are not described" [Smith].

primaryText.ACT:27:27: But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land.
primaryText.ACT:27:28: They took soundings and found twenty fathoms. After a little while, they took soundings again, and found fifteen fathoms.
primaryText.ACT:27:29: Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight.

evidence.quote: 27-29. when the fourteenth night was come--from the time they left Fair Havens.

primaryText.ACT:27:30: As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow,
primaryText.ACT:27:31: Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.”
primaryText.ACT:27:32: Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off.

evidence.quote: 30. as the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship--under cover of night.
31. Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers--the only parties now to be trusted, and whose own safety was now at stake.
32. Then the soldiers cut off the ropes of the boat--already lowered.

primaryText.ACT:27:33: While the day was coming on, Paul begged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing.
primaryText.ACT:27:34: Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.”
primaryText.ACT:27:35: When he had said this and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; then he broke it and began to eat.
primaryText.ACT:27:36: Then they all cheered up, and they also took food.
primaryText.ACT:27:37: In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.

evidence.quote: 33-37. while day was coming on--"until it should be day"; that is, in the interval between the cutting off of the boat and the approach of day, which all were "anxiously looking for" (Ac 27:29).

primaryText.ACT:27:38: When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.
primaryText.ACT:27:39: When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they decided to try to drive the ship onto it.
primaryText.ACT:27:40: Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.

evidence.quote: 38-40. when they had eaten enough, &c.--With fresh strength after the meal, they make a third and last effort to lighten the ship, not only by pumping, as before, but by throwing the whole cargo of wheat into the sea (see on Ac 27:6).

primaryText.ACT:27:41: But coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves.

evidence.quote: 41. falling into a place where two seas met--Smith thinks this refers to the channel, not more than one hundred yards broad, which separates the small island of Salmone from Malta, forming a communication between the sea inside the bay and that outside.

primaryText.ACT:27:42: The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim out and escape.
primaryText.ACT:27:43: But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land;
primaryText.ACT:27:44: and the rest should follow, some on planks and some on other things from the ship. So they all escaped safely to the land.

evidence.quote: 42-44. the soldiers' counsel was to hill the prisoners, lest any ... should escape--Roman cruelty, which made the keepers answerable for their prisoners with their own lives, is here reflected in this cruel proposal.

primaryText.ACT:28:1: When we had escaped, then they learned that the island was called Malta.

evidence.quote: 1. knew the island was called Melita--(See on Ac 27:39). The opinion that this island was not Malta to the south of Sicily, but Meleda in the Gulf of Venice--which till lately had respectable support among Competent judges--is now all but exploded; examination of all the places on the spot, and of all writings and principles bearing on th

primaryText.ACT:28:2: The natives showed us uncommon kindness; for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the present rain and because of the cold.

evidence.quote: 2. the barbarous people--so called merely as speaking neither the Greek nor the Latin language. They were originally Phoenician colonists.

primaryText.ACT:28:3: But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand.

evidence.quote: 3. when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks--"a quantity of dry sticks." The vigorous activity of Paul's character is observable in this comparatively trifling action [Webster and Wilkinson].

primaryText.ACT:28:4: When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped from the sea, yet Justice has not allowed to live.”
primaryText.ACT:28:5: However he shook off the creature into the fire, and wasn’t harmed.
primaryText.ACT:28:6: But they expected that he would have swollen or fallen down dead suddenly, but when they watched for a long time and saw nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

evidence.quote: 4-6. No doubt this man is a murderer--His chains, which they would see, might strengthen the impression.

primaryText.ACT:28:7: Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and courteously entertained us for three days.
primaryText.ACT:28:8: The father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery. Paul entered in to him, prayed, and laying his hands on him, healed him.

evidence.quote: 7-8. possessions of the chief man--"the first man."

evidence.quote: The "body" is here viewed as the instrument by which all the sins of the heart become facts of the outward life, and as itself the seat of the lower appetites;
Neither yield ye your members instruments of unrighteousness unto Sin, but yield yourselves--this is the great surrender.

To be "under the law" is, first, to be under its claim to entire obedience; and so, next under its curse for the breach of these. And as all power to obey can reach the sinner only through Grace, of which the law knows nothing, it follows that to be "under the law" is, finally, to be shut up under an inability to keep it, and consequently to be the helpless slave of sin.

that ye should be married to another, even to him that is--"was."

raised from the dead--to the intent.

that we should bring forth fruit unto God--It has been thought that the apostle should here have said that "the law died to us," not "we to the law," but that purposely inverted the figure, to avoid the harshness to Jewish ears of the death of the law [Chrysostom, Calvin, Hodge, Philippi, &c.]. But this is to mistake the apostle's design in employing this figure, which was merely to illustrate the general principle that "death dissolves legal obligation." It was essential to his argument that we, not the law, should be the dying party, since it is we that are "crucified with Christ," and not the law. This death dissolves our marriage obligation to the law, leaving us at liberty to contract a new relation--to be joined to the Risen One, in order to spiritual fruitfulness, to the glory of God

primaryText.ROM:8:35: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
primaryText.ROM:8:36: Even as it is written, “For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.”
primaryText.ROM:8:37: No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
primaryText.ROM:8:38: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers,
primaryText.ROM:8:39: nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

evidence.quote: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?--This does not mean "our love to Christ," as if, Who shall hinder us from loving Christ?
for though this be true, the word means simply, "We are pre-eminently conquerors."

primaryText.ROM:9:1: I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying, my conscience testifying with me in the Holy Spirit
primaryText.ROM:9:2: that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart.

evidence.quote: I say the truth in Christ--as if steeped in the spirit of Him who wept over impenitent and doomed Jerusalem (compare Ro 1:9; 2Co 12:19; Php 1:8).
my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost--"my conscience as quickened, illuminated, and even now under the direct operation of the Holy Ghost."

primaryText.ROM:9:3: For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers’ sake, my relatives according to the flesh

evidence.quote: and if it be understood as the language rather of "strong and indistinct emotions than of definite ideas" [Hodge], expressing passionately how he felt his whole being swallowed up in the salvation of his people, the difficulty will vanish, and we shall be reminded of the similar idea so nobly expressed by Moses (Ex 32:32).

primaryText.ROM:9:4: who are Israelites; whose is the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service, and the promises;

evidence.quote: and the covenants--"the covenants of promise" to which the Gentiles before Christ were "strangers" (Ep 2:12); meaning the one covenant with Abraham in its successive renewals (see Ga 3:16, 17).

and the service of God--or, of the sanctuary, meaning the whole divinely instituted religious service, in the celebration of which they were brought so nigh unto God.

and the promises--the great Abrahamic promises, successively unfolded, and which had their fulfilment only in Christ; (see He 7:6; Ga 3:16, 21; Ac 26:6, 7).

primaryText.ROM:9:5: of whom are the fathers, and from whom is Christ as concerning the flesh, who is over all, God, blessed forever. Amen.

evidence.quote: It remains then, that we have here no doxology at all, but a naked statement of fact, that while Christ is "of" the Israelitish nation "as concerning the flesh," He is, in another respect, "God over all, blessed for ever."

primaryText.ROM:9:6: But it is not as though the word of God has come to nothing. For they are not all Israel that are of Israel.

evidence.quote: but not all that belong to the natural seed, and go under the name of 'Israel,' are the Israel of God's irrevocable choice.
the Election treated of in the body of this chapter is national, not personal Election, and consequently is Election merely to religious advantages, not to eternal salvation.

primaryText.ROM:9:7: Neither, because they are Abraham’s offspring, are they all children. But, “your offspring will be accounted as from Isaac.”
primaryText.ROM:9:8: That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as heirs.
primaryText.ROM:9:9: For this is a word of promise: “At the appointed time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.”

evidence.quote: but--the true election are such of Abraham's seed as God unconditionally chooses, as exemplified in that promise.

primaryText.ROM:9:10: Not only so, but Rebekah also conceived by one, by our father Isaac.
primaryText.ROM:9:11: For being not yet born, neither having done anything good or bad, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls,
primaryText.ROM:9:12: it was said to her, “The elder will serve the younger.”
primaryText.ROM:9:13: Even as it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

evidence.quote: But there could be no such reason in the case of Rebecca, Isaac's only wife; for the choice of her son Jacob was the choice of one of two sons by the same mother and of the younger in preference to the elder, and before either of them was born, and consequently before either had done good or evil to be a ground of preference: and all to show that the sole ground of distinction lay in the unconditional choice of God--"not of works, but of Him that calleth."

primaryText.ROM:9:14: What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!

evidence.quote: This is the first of two objections to the foregoing doctrine, that God chooses one and rejects another, not on account of their works, but purely in the exercise of His own good pleasure: "This doctrine is inconsistent with the justice of God."

primaryText.ROM:9:15: For he said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”

evidence.quote: There can be no unrighteousness in God's choosing whom He will, for to Moses He expressly claims the right to do so." Yet it is worthy of notice that this is expressed in the positive rather than the negative form: not, "I will have mercy on none but whom I will"; but, "I will have mercy on whomsoever I will."

primaryText.ROM:9:16: So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.

evidence.quote: Both these are indispensable to salvation, yet salvation is owing to neither, but is purely "of God that showeth mercy."

primaryText.ROM:9:17: For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I caused you to be raised up, that I might show in you my power, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”

evidence.quote: But "God did not make Pharaoh wicked; He only forbore to make him good, by the exercise of special and altogether unmerited grace" [Hodge].

It was not that Pharaoh was worse than others that he was so dealt with, but "in order that he might become a monument of the penal justice of God, and it was with a view to this that God provided that the evil which was in him should be manifested in this definite form" [Olshausen].

primaryText.ROM:9:18: So then, he has mercy on whom he desires, and he hardens whom he desires.

evidence.quote:
Therefore hath he--"So then he hath." The result then is that He hath

mercy on whom he will have mercy, and whom he will he hardeneth--by judicially abandoning them to the hardening influence of sin itself (Psa 81:11,

primaryText.ROM:9:19: You will say then to me, “Why does he still find fault? For who withstands his will?”

evidence.quote: This objection shows quite as conclusively as the former the real nature of the doctrine objected to--that it is Election and Non-election to eternal salvation prior to any difference of personal character; this is the only doctrine that could suggest the objection here stated, and to this doctrine the objection is plausible.

primaryText.ROM:9:20: But indeed, O man, who are you to reply against God? Will the thing formed ask him who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?”
primaryText.ROM:9:21: Or hasn’t the potter a right over the clay, from the same lump to make one part a vessel for honor, and another for dishonor?

evidence.quote:
Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made--"didst thou make"

me thus?--(Is 45:9).

primaryText.ROM:9:22: What if God, willing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction,
primaryText.ROM:9:23: and that he might make known the riches of his glory on vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory—

evidence.quote: the vessels of wrath--that is, "destined to wrath"; just as "vessels of mercy," in Ro 9:23, mean "vessels destined to mercy"; compare Ep 2:3, "children of wrath."
the apostle would have it remarked that God "endures with much long-suffering" those objects of His righteous displeasure.

primaryText.ROM:9:24: us, whom he also called, not from the Jews only, but also from the Gentiles?

evidence.quote: Here for the first title in this chapter the calling of the Gentiles is introduced; all before having respect, not to the substitution of the called Gentiles for the rejected Jews, but to the choice of one portion and the rejection of another of the same Israel.

primaryText.ROM:9:25: As he says also in Hosea, “I will call them ‘my people,’ which were not my people; and her ‘beloved,’ who was not beloved.”

evidence.quote: quoted, though not quite to the letter, from Ho 2:23, a passage relating immediately, not to the heathen, but to the kingdom of the ten tribes; but since they had sunk to the level of the heathen, who were "not God's people," and in that sense "not beloved," the apostle legitimately applies it to the heathen

primaryText.ROM:9:26: “It will be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘children of the living God.’”

evidence.quote: The expression, "in the place where ... there," seems designed only to give greater emphasis to the gracious change here announced, from divine exclusion to divine admission to the privileges of the people of God.

primaryText.ROM:9:27: Isaiah cries concerning Israel, “If the number of the children of Israel are as the sand of the sea, it is the remnant who will be saved;
primaryText.ROM:9:28: for he will finish the work and cut it short in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short work upon the earth.”
primaryText.ROM:9:29: As Isaiah has said before, “Unless the Lord of Armies had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and would have been made like Gomorrah.”

evidence.quote: remnant--that is, the elect remnant only shall be saved.

primaryText.ROM:9:30: What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, who didn’t follow after righteousness, attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith;
primaryText.ROM:9:31: but Israel, following after a law of righteousness, didn’t arrive at the law of righteousness.

evidence.quote: As we have seen that "the righteousness of faith" is the righteousness which justifies (see on Ro 3:22, &c.), this verse must mean that "the Gentiles, who while strangers to Christ were quite indifferent about acceptance with God, having embraced the Gospel as soon as it was preached to them, experienced the blessedness of a justified state."

primaryText.ROM:9:32: Why? Because they didn’t seek it by faith, but as it were by works of the law. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,
primaryText.ROM:9:33: even as it is written, “Behold, I lay in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock of offense; and no one who believes in him will be disappointed.”

evidence.quote:
by the works of the law--as if it were thus attainable, which justification is not: Since, therefore, it is attainable only by faith, they missed it.

for--it is doubtful if this particle was originally in the text.

they stumbled at that stumbling-stone--better, "against the stone of stumbling," meaning Christ.

primaryText.ROM:10:1: Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God is for Israel, that they may be saved.

evidence.quote: is, that they may be saved--"for their salvation." Having before poured forth the anguish of his soul at the general unbelief of his nation and its dreadful consequences (Ro 9:1-3), he here expresses in the most emphatic terms his desire and prayer for their salvation.

primaryText.ROM:10:2: For I testify about them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

evidence.quote: He alludes to this well-meaning of his people, notwithstanding their spiritual blindness, not certainly to excuse their rejection of Christ and rage against His saints, but as some ground of hope regarding them.

primaryText.ROM:10:3: For being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they didn’t subject themselves to the righteousness of God.

evidence.quote: to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God--The apostle views the general rejection of Christ by the nation as one act.

primaryText.ROM:10:4: For Christ is the fulfillment of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

evidence.quote:
For Christ is the end--the object or aim.

of the law for--justifying

righteousness to every one that believeth--that is, contains within Himself all that the law demands for the justification of such as embrace Him, whether Jew or Gentile (Ga

primaryText.ROM:10:5: For Moses writes about the righteousness of the law, “The one who does them will live by them.”

evidence.quote: shall live in them--(Le 18:5). This is the one way of justification and life--by "the righteousness which is of (or, by our own obedience to) the law."

primaryText.ROM:10:6: But the righteousness which is of faith says this, “Don’t say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down);

evidence.quote: First, We need not go to heaven, to search the records there, or to enquire into the secrets of the divine counsel. It is true Christ is in heaven; but we may be justified and saved without going thither, to fetch him thence, or sending a special messenger to him.

primaryText.ROM:10:7: or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.)”

evidence.quote: Secondly, We need not go to the deep, to fetch Christ out of the grave, or from the state of the dead: Into the deep, to bring up Christ from the dead.

primaryText.ROM:10:8: But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart;” that is, the word of faith which we preach:

evidence.quote: Christ is nigh thee, for the word is nigh thee: nigh thee indeed: it is in thy mouth, and in thy heart; there is no difficulty in understanding, believing, and owning it.

primaryText.ROM:10:9: that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.

evidence.quote: Confessing the Lord Jesus—openly professing relation to him and dependence on him, as our prince and Saviour, owning Christianity in the face of all the allurements and affrightments of this world, standing by him in all weathers.

primaryText.ROM:10:10: For with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.

evidence.quote: This is further illustrated (v. 10), and the order inverted, because there must first be faith in the heart before there can be an acceptable confession with the mouth.
Confessing the Lord Jesus—openly professing relation to him and dependence on him

primaryText.ROM:10:11: For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes in him will not be disappointed.”

evidence.quote: Whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed--Here, as in Ro 9:33, the quotation is from the Septuagint, which renders those words of the original, "shall not make haste" (that is, fly for escape, as from conscious danger), "shall not be put to shame," which comes to the same thing.

primaryText.ROM:10:12: For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, and is rich to all who call on him.

evidence.quote: There is not one God to the Jews who is more kind, and another to the Gentiles who is less kind; but he is the same to all, a common father to all mankind.

primaryText.ROM:10:13: For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

evidence.quote: This extent, this undifferencing extent, of the promise both to Jews and Gentiles he thinks should not be surprising, for it was foretold by the prophet, Joel ii. 32. Calling upon the name of the Lord is here put for all practical religion.

primaryText.ROM:10:14: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?
primaryText.ROM:10:15: And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!”

evidence.quote: But this calling implies believing, and believing hearing, and hearing preaching, and preaching a mission to preach: Why, then, take ye it so ill, O children of Abraham, that in obedience to our heavenly mission (Ac 26:16-18) we preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ?

primaryText.ROM:10:16: But they didn’t all listen to the glad news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our report?”
primaryText.ROM:10:17: So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

evidence.quote: For Esaias saith, Lord, who hath believed our report?--that is,"Where shall one find a believer?" The prophet speaks as if next to none would believe: The apostle softens this into "They have not all believed."

primaryText.ROM:10:18: But I say, didn’t they hear? Yes, most certainly, “Their sound went out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.”

evidence.quote: These beautiful words are from Psa 19:4. Whether the apostle quoted them as in their primary intention applicable to his subject (as Olshausen, Alford, &c.), or only "used scriptural language to express his own ideas, as is done involuntarily almost by every preacher in every sermon" [Hodge], expositors are not agreed.

primaryText.ROM:10:19: But I ask, didn’t Israel know? First Moses says, “I will provoke you to jealousy with that which is no nation. I will make you angry with a nation void of understanding.”

evidence.quote: But I say, Did not Israel know?--know, from their own Scriptures, of God's intention to bring in the Gentiles?

primaryText.ROM:10:20: Isaiah is very bold and says, “I was found by those who didn’t seek me. I was revealed to those who didn’t ask for me.”

evidence.quote: That the calling of the Gentiles was meant by these words of the prophet (Is 65:1) is manifest from what immediately follows, "I said, Behold Me, behold Me, unto a nation that was not called by My name."

primaryText.ROM:10:21: But about Israel he says, “All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

evidence.quote:
my hands--the attitude of gracious entreaty.

unto a disobedient and gainsaying people--These words, which immediately follow the announcement just quoted of the calling of the Gentiles, were enough to forewarn the Jews both of God's purpose to eject them from their privileges, in favor of the Gentiles, and of the cause of it on their own part.

primaryText.ROM:11:1: I ask then, did God reject his people? May it never be! For I also am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.

evidence.quote: First, Israel is not wholly cast away.

primaryText.ROM:11:2: God didn’t reject his people, whom he foreknew. Or don’t you know what the Scripture says about Elijah? How he pleads with God against Israel:
primaryText.ROM:11:3: “Lord, they have killed your prophets. They have broken down your altars. I am left alone, and they seek my life.”
primaryText.ROM:11:4: But how does God answer him? “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”

evidence.quote: not cast away his people--that is, wholly

primaryText.ROM:11:5: Even so too at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.

evidence.quote: There is now, as there was then, a faithful remnant; not however of persons naturally better than the unbelieving mass, but of persons graciously chosen to salvation.

primaryText.ROM:11:6: And if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. But if it is of works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work.

evidence.quote: salvation cannot be of any combination or mixture of both, but must be wholly either of the one or of the other.

primaryText.ROM:11:10: Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see. Always keep their backs bent.”
primaryText.ROM:11:7: What then? That which Israel seeks for, that he didn’t obtain, but the chosen ones obtained it, and the rest were hardened.
primaryText.ROM:11:8: According as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, to this very day.”
primaryText.ROM:11:9: David says, “Let their table be made a snare, a trap, a stumbling block, and a retribution to them.

evidence.quote: the election (the elect remnant of Israel) found it, and the rest were hardened," or judicially given over to the "hardness of their own hearts.

primaryText.ROM:11:11: I ask then, did they stumble that they might fall? May it never be! But by their fall salvation has come to the Gentiles, to provoke them to jealousy.

evidence.quote: emulation is a legitimate stimulus to what is good.

primaryText.ROM:11:12: Now if their fall is the riches of the world, and their loss the riches of the Gentiles, how much more their fullness!

evidence.quote: their full recovery (see on Ro 11:26); that is, "If an event so untoward as Israel's fall was the occasion of such unspeakable good to the Gentile world, of how much greater good may we expect an event so blessed as their full recovery to be productive?

primaryText.ROM:11:13: For I speak to you who are Gentiles. Since then as I am an apostle to Gentiles, I glorify my ministry,
primaryText.ROM:11:14: if by any means I may provoke to jealousy those who are my flesh, and may save some of them.

evidence.quote:
I magnify--"glorify"

mine office

primaryText.ROM:11:15: For if the rejection of them is the reconciling of the world, what would their acceptance be, but life from the dead?
primaryText.ROM:11:16: If the first fruit is holy, so is the lump. If the root is holy, so are the branches.

evidence.quote: they were cast away, though neither totally nor finally, and it is of this partial and temporary rejection that the apostle here speaks.

the argument of the apostle is, that as the separation unto God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, from the rest of mankind, as the parent stem of their race, was as real an offering of first-fruits as that which hallowed the produce of the earth, so, in the divine estimation, it was as real a separation of the mass or "lump" of that nation in all time to God. The figure of the "root" and its "branches" is of like import--the consecration of the one of them extending to the other.

primaryText.ROM:11:17: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became partaker with them of the root and of the richness of the olive tree,
primaryText.ROM:11:18: don’t boast over the branches. But if you boast, remember that it is not you who support the root, but the root supports you.

evidence.quote: the rich grace secured by covenant to the true seed of Abraham.

primaryText.ROM:11:19: You will say then, “Branches were broken off, that I might be grafted in.”
primaryText.ROM:11:20: True; by their unbelief they were broken off, and you stand by your faith. Don’t be conceited, but fear;
primaryText.ROM:11:21: for if God didn’t spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.

evidence.quote: Thou wilt say then--as a plea for boasting.

primaryText.ROM:11:22: See then the goodness and severity of God. Toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, goodness, if you continue in his goodness; otherwise you also will be cut off.
primaryText.ROM:11:23: They also, if they don’t continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.
primaryText.ROM:11:24: For if you were cut out of that which is by nature a wild olive tree, and were grafted contrary to nature into a good olive tree, how much more will these, which are the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree?

evidence.quote: in believing dependence on that pure goodness which made thee what thou art.

so the restoration of Israel, when they shall be brought to believe in Jesus, is a thing far more in the line of what we should expect, than the admission of the Gentiles to a standing which they never before enjoyed.

primaryText.ROM:11:25: For I don’t desire you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you won’t be wise in your own conceits, that a partial hardening has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in,
primaryText.ROM:11:26: and so all Israel will be saved. Even as it is written, “There will come out of Zion the Deliverer, and he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.
primaryText.ROM:11:27: This is my covenant with them, when I will take away their sins.”

evidence.quote: It can only mean the ultimate ingathering of Israel as a nation, in contrast with the present "remnant."

primaryText.ROM:11:28: Concerning the Good News, they are enemies for your sake. But concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers’ sake.
primaryText.ROM:11:29: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.

evidence.quote: they are beloved--even in their state of exclusion for the fathers' sakes.

primaryText.ROM:11:30: For as you in time past were disobedient to God, but now have obtained mercy by their disobedience,
primaryText.ROM:11:31: even so these also have now been disobedient, that by the mercy shown to you they may also obtain mercy.
primaryText.ROM:11:32: For God has bound all to disobedience, that he might have mercy on all.

evidence.quote: the Gentiles first, and after them the Jews [Fritzsche, Tholuck, Olshausen, De Wette, Philippi, Stuart, Hodge].

primaryText.ROM:11:33: Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out!
primaryText.ROM:11:34: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?”
primaryText.ROM:11:35: “Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him again?”
primaryText.ROM:11:36: For of him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.

evidence.quote: Oh, the depth, &c.--The apostle now yields himself up to the admiring contemplation of the grandeur of that divine plan which he had sketched out.
For who hath known the mind of the Lord?--See Job 15:8; Jr 23:18.
He challenges any to prove God a debtor to him (v. 35): Who hath first given to him?

For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom--"to Him"

be glory for ever.

primaryText.ROM:12:1: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.

evidence.quote: your bodies--that is, "yourselves in the body," considered as the organ of the inner life.

primaryText.ROM:12:2: Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

evidence.quote: not by a mere outward disconformity to the ungodly world, many of whose actions in themselves may be virtuous and praiseworthy; but by such an inward spiritual transformation as makes the whole life new--new in its motives and ends

primaryText.ROM:12:3: For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.

evidence.quote: as God hath given to each his particular capacity to take in the gifts and graces which He designs for the general good.

primaryText.ROM:12:4: For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
primaryText.ROM:12:5: so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,

evidence.quote: The same diversity and yet unity obtains in the body of Christ, whereof all believers are the several members, as in the natural body.

primaryText.ROM:12:6: having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
primaryText.ROM:12:7: or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
primaryText.ROM:12:8: or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

evidence.quote: all the gifts of believers alike are viewed as communications of mere grace

primaryText.ROM:12:9: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.

evidence.quote: Abhor the one, and cling, with deepest sympathy, to the other.

primaryText.ROM:12:10: In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,

evidence.quote: In brotherly love be affectionate one to another; in [giving, or showing] honor, outdoing each other." The word rendered "prefer" means rather "to go before," "take the lead," that is, "show an example."

primaryText.ROM:12:11: not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
primaryText.ROM:12:12: rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
primaryText.ROM:12:13: contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.

evidence.quote: serving the Lord--that is, the Lord Jesus

primaryText.ROM:12:14: Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse.

evidence.quote:
Bless--that is, Call down by prayer a blessing on.

them which persecute you

primaryText.ROM:12:15: Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.
primaryText.ROM:12:16: Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.

evidence.quote:
Mind not--"not minding"

high things--that is, Cherish not ambitious or aspiring purposes and desires. As this springs from selfish severance of our own interests and objects from those of our brethren, so it is quite incompatible with the spirit inculcated in the preceding clause.

but condescend--"condescending"

to men of low estate--or (as some render the words), "inclining unto the things that be lowly." But we prefer the former.

primaryText.ROM:12:17: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
primaryText.ROM:12:18: If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

evidence.quote:
Recompense--"Recompensing," &c.--(See on Ro 12:14).

Provide--"Providing"

things honest--"honorable"

in the sight of all men--The idea (which is from Pr 3:4) is the care which Christians should take so to demean themselves as to command the respect of all

If it be possible--that is, If others will let you.

It is of Magistracy in general, considered as a divine ordinance, that this is spoken: and the statement applies equally to all forms of government, from an unchecked despotism--such as flourished when this was written, under the Emperor Nero--to a pure democracy. The inalienable right of all subjects to endeavor to alter or improve the form of government under which they live is left untouched here. But since Christians were constantly charged with turning the world upside down, and since there certainly were elements enough in Christianity of moral and social revolution to give plausibility to the charge, and tempt noble spirits, crushed under misgovernment, to take redress into their own hands, it was of special importance that the pacific, submissive, loyal spirit of those Christians who resided at the great seat of political power, should furnish a visible refutation of this charge.

primaryText.PRO:1:20: Wisdom calls aloud in the street. She utters her voice in the public squares.
primaryText.PRO:1:21: She calls at the head of noisy places. At the entrance of the city gates, she utters her words:
primaryText.PRO:1:22: “How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity? How long will mockers delight themselves in mockery, and fools hate knowledge?
primaryText.PRO:1:23: Turn at my reproof. Behold, I will pour out my spirit on you. I will make known my words to you.

evidence.quote:
Some interpreters regard this address as the language of the
Son of God under the name of Wisdom (compare

Lu 11:49).

Others think that wisdom, as the divine attribute specially employed in
acts of counsel and admonition, is here personified, and represents
God. In either case the address is a most solemn and divine admonition,
whose matter and spirit are eminently evangelical and impressive (see
on

Pr 8:1).

Wisdom--literally, "Wisdoms," the plural used either because of the
unusual sense, or as indicative of the great excellency of wisdom
(compare

Pr 9:1).

streets--or most public places, not secretly.

The publicity further indicated by terms designating places of
most common resort.

simple ones--(Compare

Pr 1:4).

simplicity--implying ignorance.

scorners--

(Ps 1:1)

--who despise, as well as reject, truth.

fools--Though a different word is used from that of

Pr 1:7,

yet it is of the same meaning.

reproof--implying conviction deserving it (compare

Joh 16:8,

Margin).

pour out--abundantly impart.

my spirit--whether of wisdom personified, or of Christ, a divine agent.

primaryText.PRO:1:24: Because I have called, and you have refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no one has paid attention;
primaryText.PRO:1:25: but you have ignored all my counsel, and wanted none of my reproof;
primaryText.PRO:1:26: I also will laugh at your disaster. I will mock when calamity overtakes you,
primaryText.PRO:1:27: when calamity overtakes you like a storm, when your disaster comes on like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish come on you.

evidence.quote:
Some interpreters regard this address as the language of the
Son of God under the name of Wisdom (compare

Lu 11:49).

Others think that wisdom, as the divine attribute specially employed in
acts of counsel and admonition, is here personified, and represents
God. In either case the address is a most solemn and divine admonition,
whose matter and spirit are eminently evangelical and impressive (see
on

Pr 8:1).

Wisdom--literally, "Wisdoms," the plural used either because of the
unusual sense, or as indicative of the great excellency of wisdom
(compare

Pr 9:1).

streets--or most public places, not secretly.

stretched . . . hand--Earnestness, especially in beseeching, is
denoted by the figure (compare

Job 11:13;
Ps 68:31; 88:9).

set at naught--rejected as of no value.

would none of--literally, "were not willing or inclined to it."

In their extreme distress He will not only refuse help, but
aggravate it by derision.

fear--the object of it.

desolation--literally, "a tumultuous noise," denoting their utter
confusion.

destruction--or calamity

(Pr 1:26)

compared to a whirlwind, as to fatal rapidity.

distress--

(Ps 4:1; 44:11).

anguish--a state of inextricable oppression, the deepest despair.

primaryText.PRO:1:28: Then they will call on me, but I will not answer. They will seek me diligently, but they will not find me,
primaryText.PRO:1:29: because they hated knowledge, and didn’t choose the fear of the LORD.
primaryText.PRO:1:30: They wanted none of my counsel. They despised all my reproof.

evidence.quote:
Some interpreters regard this address as the language of the
Son of God under the name of Wisdom (compare

Lu 11:49).

Others think that wisdom, as the divine attribute specially employed in
acts of counsel and admonition, is here personified, and represents
God. In either case the address is a most solemn and divine admonition,
whose matter and spirit are eminently evangelical and impressive (see
on

Pr 8:1).

Wisdom--literally, "Wisdoms," the plural used either because of the
unusual sense, or as indicative of the great excellency of wisdom
(compare

Pr 9:1).

streets--or most public places, not secretly.

Now no prayers or most diligent seeking will avail

(Pr 8:17).
The sinner's infatuated rejection brings his ruin.

primaryText.PRO:1:31: Therefore they will eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own schemes.
primaryText.PRO:1:32: For the backsliding of the simple will kill them. The careless ease of fools will destroy them.

evidence.quote:
Some interpreters regard this address as the language of the
Son of God under the name of Wisdom (compare

Lu 11:49).

Others think that wisdom, as the divine attribute specially employed in
acts of counsel and admonition, is here personified, and represents
God. In either case the address is a most solemn and divine admonition,
whose matter and spirit are eminently evangelical and impressive (see
on

Pr 8:1).

Wisdom--literally, "Wisdoms," the plural used either because of the
unusual sense, or as indicative of the great excellency of wisdom
(compare

Pr 9:1).

streets--or most public places, not secretly.

turning away--that is, from the call of

Pr 1:23.

simple--as in

Pr 1:22.

prosperity--quiet, implying indifference.

primaryText.PRO:1:33: But whoever listens to me will dwell securely, and will be at ease, without fear of harm.”

evidence.quote:
Some interpreters regard this address as the language of the
Son of God under the name of Wisdom (compare

Lu 11:49).

Others think that wisdom, as the divine attribute specially employed in
acts of counsel and admonition, is here personified, and represents
God. In either case the address is a most solemn and divine admonition,
whose matter and spirit are eminently evangelical and impressive (see
on

Pr 8:1).

Wisdom--literally, "Wisdoms," the plural used either because of the
unusual sense, or as indicative of the great excellency of wisdom
(compare

Pr 9:1).

streets--or most public places, not secretly.

dwell safely--literally, "in confidence"

(De 12:10).

be quiet--or at ease, in real prosperity.

from fear--without fear.

primaryText.PRO:2:1: My son, if you will receive my words, and store up my commandments within you,
primaryText.PRO:2:2: so as to turn your ear to wisdom, and apply your heart to understanding;
primaryText.PRO:2:3: yes, if you call out for discernment, and lift up your voice for understanding;
primaryText.PRO:2:4: if you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures;
primaryText.PRO:2:5: then you will understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God.

evidence.quote:
Diligence in hearing and praying for instruction must be used to
secure the great principle of godliness, the fear of God.

hide . . . with thee--lay up in store (compare

Pr 7:1).

Listen attentively and reflect seriously

(Pr 1:24;
Ps 130:2).

understanding--right perception of truth.

Yea, if--literally, "When if," that is, in such a case.

knowledge--or, "discrimination."

understanding--as in

Pr 2:2.
There must be earnest prayer and effort.

understand--or, "perceive intelligently."

find--obtain.

primaryText.PRO:2:6: For the LORD gives wisdom. Out of his mouth comes knowledge and understanding.
primaryText.PRO:2:7: He lays up sound wisdom for the upright. He is a shield to those who walk in integrity,
primaryText.PRO:2:8: that he may guard the paths of justice, and preserve the way of his saints.
primaryText.PRO:2:9: Then you will understand righteousness and justice, equity and every good path.

evidence.quote:
For--God is ready

(Jas 1:5; 4:8).

out of his mouth--by revelation from Him.

sound wisdom--literally, "substance," opposed to what is
fictitious. According to the context, this may be assistance, as here
corresponding with

buckler--or safety, or wisdom, which procures it (compare

Pr 3:21; 8:14; 18:1;
Job 6:13; 12:13).

layeth up--provides, ever ready.

keepeth . . . way--God defends the right way, and those in it.

saints--objects of favor (compare

Ps 4:3,

&c.). He guides and guards them.

Then--emphatic, in such a case.

righteousness . . . path--all parts of duty to God and man.

primaryText.PRO:2:10: For wisdom will enter into your heart. Knowledge will be pleasant to your soul.
primaryText.PRO:2:11: Discretion will watch over you. Understanding will keep you,
primaryText.PRO:2:12: to deliver you from the way of evil, from the men who speak perverse things,
primaryText.PRO:2:13: who forsake the paths of uprightness, to walk in the ways of darkness,
primaryText.PRO:2:14: who rejoice to do evil, and delight in the perverseness of evil,
primaryText.PRO:2:15: who are crooked in their ways, and wayward in their paths,

evidence.quote:
Idea of

Pr 2:9,

amplified; on terms, compare

Pr 2:2
and Pr 2:4.

To deliver--as from great danger

(Pr 6:5).

way . . . man--

(Ps 1:1).

froward things--perversity

(Pr 6:14; 23:23),

what is opposed to truth.

paths of uprightness--or, "plainness."

walk--habitually act;

and that with pleasure, in ignorance of good and pursuit of evil.

frowardness--Not only their own perversity, but that of others is their
delight. They love most the worst things.

crooked--tortuous, unprincipled.

froward--literally, (they) are going back, not only aside from right,
but opposite to it.

primaryText.PRO:2:16: to deliver you from the strange woman, even from the foreigner who flatters with her words,
primaryText.PRO:2:17: who forsakes the friend of her youth, and forgets the covenant of her God;
primaryText.PRO:2:18: for her house leads down to death, her paths to the departed spirits.
primaryText.PRO:2:19: None who go to her return again, neither do they attain to the paths of life.

evidence.quote:
Deliverance from another danger.

the strange woman--This term is often used for harlot, or loose woman

(Jud 11:1, 2),

married

(Pr 7:5, 19)

or not

(1Ki 11:1),

so called, because such were, perhaps at first, foreigners, though
"strange" may also denote whatever is opposed to right or proper, as
"strange fire"

(Nu 3:4);

"strange incense"

(Ex 30:9).

flattereth--literally, "smooths."

her words--

(Ps 5:9).

guide . . . youth--lawful husband

(Jer 3:4).

covenant . . . God--of marriage made in God's name.

inclineth--sinks down (compare

Nu 13:31).

the dead--or shades of the departed

(Ps 88:10).

that is, such as remain impenitent (compare

Ec 7:26).

paths of life--

(Ps 16:11),

opposed to paths unto the dead.

primaryText.PRO:2:20: Therefore walk in the way of good men, and keep the paths of the righteous.
primaryText.PRO:2:21: For the upright will dwell in the land. The perfect will remain in it.
primaryText.PRO:2:22: But the wicked will be cut off from the land. The treacherous will be rooted out of it.

evidence.quote:
That . . . way of good--that is, Such is the object of these
warnings.

transgressors--or impious rebels (compare

Jer 9:2).

rooted out--utterly destroyed, as trees plucked up by the roots.

primaryText.PRO:3:1: My son, don’t forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments,
primaryText.PRO:3:2: for they will add to you length of days, years of life, and peace.
primaryText.PRO:3:3: Don’t let kindness and truth forsake you. Bind them around your neck. Write them on the tablet of your heart.
primaryText.PRO:3:4: So you will find favor, and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

evidence.quote:
law [and] commandments--all divine instructions
(see on

Ps 119:1

and

Ps 119:4).

let thine heart keep--or sincerely observe

(Pr 4:13; 5:2).

length . . . life--often promised as blessings

(Ps 21:4; 91:16).

peace--includes prosperity

(Ps 125:5).

add--abound to thee.

mercy and truth--God's faithfulness to His promises is often
expressed by these terms

(Ps 25:10; 57:3).

As attributes of men, they express integrity in a wide sense

(Pr 16:6; 20:28).

bind . . . write . . . heart--outwardly adorn and inwardly govern
motives.

favour--grace, amiability

(Pr 22:11;
Ps 45:2);

united with this,

a good understanding--(Compare Margin), a discrimination, which
secures success.

in the sight . . . man--such as God and man approve.

primaryText.PRO:3:5: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.
primaryText.PRO:3:6: In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.

evidence.quote:
Trust . . . heart--This is the center and marrow of true wisdom

(Pr 22:19; 28:25).

The positive duty has its corresponding negation in the admonition
against self-confidence.

ways--

(Ps 1:1).

acknowledge--by seeking His wise aid

(Pr 16:3;
Ps 37:5;
Jer 9:23, 24).

direct--literally, "make plain" (compare

Heb 12:13).

primaryText.PRO:3:7: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear the LORD, and depart from evil.
primaryText.PRO:3:8: It will be health to your body, and nourishment to your bones.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 27:2;
Ro 12:16).

fear . . . evil--reverentially regarding His law.

It--This conduct.

health--(Compare Margin).

to thy navel--for all the organs of nourishment.

marrow--(Compare Margin).

bones--frame of body. True piety promotes bodily health.

primaryText.PRO:3:10: so your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.
primaryText.PRO:3:9: Honor the LORD with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase;

evidence.quote:
presses--or wine fats

(Joe 2:24; 3:13).

primaryText.PRO:3:11: My son, don’t despise the LORD’s discipline, neither be weary of his correction;
primaryText.PRO:3:12: for whom the LORD loves, he corrects, even as a father reproves the son in whom he delights.

evidence.quote:
The true intent of afflictions considered; they do not
contradict the assertion of the blessed state of the pious

(Job 5:17;
Heb 12:5, 6).

he delighteth--or receiveth as denoting reconciliation regarding
the offense which produced chastisement.

primaryText.PRO:3:13: Happy is the man who finds wisdom, the man who gets understanding.
primaryText.PRO:3:14: For her good profit is better than getting silver, and her return is better than fine gold.
primaryText.PRO:3:15: She is more precious than rubies. None of the things you can desire are to be compared to her.

evidence.quote:
findeth--literally, "reaches," or "obtains by seeking."

getteth--literally, "draws out," as metals by digging.

The figure of

Pr 3:13

carried out.

it--that is, wisdom.

merchandise of silver--acquisition by trading.

fine gold--dug gold, solid as a nugget.
rubies--gems, or pearls.

primaryText.PRO:3:16: Length of days is in her right hand. In her left hand are riches and honor.
primaryText.PRO:3:17: Her ways are ways of pleasantness. All her paths are peace.
primaryText.PRO:3:18: She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her. Happy is everyone who retains her.

evidence.quote: Her ways--such as she directs us to take.

Wisdom allegorized as

a tree of life--

(Ge 2:9; 3:22)

whose fruit preserves life, gives all that makes living a blessing.

primaryText.PRO:3:19: By wisdom the LORD founded the earth. By understanding, he established the heavens.
primaryText.PRO:3:20: By his knowledge, the depths were broken up, and the skies drop down the dew.

evidence.quote:
The place of wisdom in the economy of creation and providence
commends it to men, who, in proportion to their finite powers, may
possess this invaluable attribute, and are thus encouraged by the divine
example of its use to seek its possession.

primaryText.PRO:3:21: My son, let them not depart from your eyes. Keep sound wisdom and discretion,
primaryText.PRO:3:22: so they will be life to your soul, and grace for your neck.
primaryText.PRO:3:23: Then you shall walk in your way securely. Your foot won’t stumble.
primaryText.PRO:3:24: When you lie down, you will not be afraid. Yes, you will lie down, and your sleep will be sweet.

evidence.quote:
sound wisdom--(compare

Pr 2:7).

let . . . eyes--that is, these words of instruction.

assign reasons in their value for happiness and ornament,
guidance and support in dangers, both when waking and sleeping.

primaryText.PRO:3:25: Don’t be afraid of sudden fear, neither of the desolation of the wicked, when it comes;
primaryText.PRO:3:26: for the LORD will be your confidence, and will keep your foot from being taken.

evidence.quote:
Be not--or, "You shall not be."

sudden fear--what causes it

(Pr 1:27),

any unlooked-for evil

(Ps 46:3; 91:12;
1Pe 3:14).

desolation--

(Pr 1:27).

The reason; such as are objects of God's favor.

be thy confidence--literally, "in thy confidence," in the source of thy
strength (compare

Na 3:9,

for the same construction, Hebrew).

primaryText.PRO:3:27: Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it.
primaryText.PRO:3:28: Don’t say to your neighbor, “Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,” when you have it by you.

evidence.quote:
Promptly fulfil all obligations both of justice and charity
(compare

Jas 2:15, 16).

primaryText.PRO:3:29: Don’t devise evil against your neighbor, since he dwells securely by you.
primaryText.PRO:3:30: Don’t strive with a man without cause, if he has done you no harm.
primaryText.PRO:3:31: Don’t envy the man of violence. Choose none of his ways.

evidence.quote: Do not abuse confidence and avoid litigation.

oppressor--or man of mischief. The destiny of successful evildoers
warns against desiring their lot

(Ps 37:1, 2, 35, 36).

primaryText.PRO:3:32: For the perverse is an abomination to the LORD, but his friendship is with the upright.
primaryText.PRO:3:33: The LORD’s curse is in the house of the wicked, but he blesses the habitation of the righteous.
primaryText.PRO:3:34: Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.
primaryText.PRO:3:35: The wise will inherit glory, but shame will be the promotion of fools.

evidence.quote:
Reasons for the warning.

froward--

(Pr 2:15).

secret . . . righteous--in their communion

(Am 3:7).
curse . . . wicked--It abides with them, and will be manifested.

The retribution of sinners, as in

Ps 18:26.

inherit--as a portion.

shame--or disgrace, as opposed to honor.

promotion--(Compare Margin); as honor for well-doing makes men
conspicuous, so fools are signalized by disgrace.

primaryText.PRO:4:1: Listen, sons, to a father’s instruction. Pay attention and know understanding;
primaryText.PRO:4:2: for I give you sound learning. Don’t forsake my law.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 1:8).

to know--in order to know.

doctrine--the matter of learning

(Pr 1:5),

such as he had received

(La 3:1).

primaryText.PRO:4:3: For I was a son to my father, tender and an only child in the sight of my mother.
primaryText.PRO:4:4: He taught me, and said to me: “Let your heart retain my words. Keep my commandments, and live.

evidence.quote:
father's son--emphatic, a son specially regarded, and so called
tender, as an object of special care (compare

1Ch 22:7; 29:1);

an idea further expressed by

only beloved--or, "as an only son"

(Ge 22:2),

though he had brothers (see on

1Ch 3:5).

He taught--or directed me.

retain--as well as receive.

keep . . . and live--observe, that you may live

(Pr 7:2).

primaryText.PRO:4:5: Get wisdom. Get understanding. Don’t forget, and don’t deviate from the words of my mouth.
primaryText.PRO:4:6: Don’t forsake her, and she will preserve you. Love her, and she will keep you.
primaryText.PRO:4:7: Wisdom is supreme. Get wisdom. Yes, though it costs all your possessions, get understanding.
primaryText.PRO:4:8: Esteem her, and she will exalt you. She will bring you to honor when you embrace her.
primaryText.PRO:4:9: She will give to your head a garland of grace. She will deliver a crown of splendor to you.”

evidence.quote:
Get--as a possession not to be given up.

neither decline--that is, from obeying my word.

Not only accept but love wisdom, who will keep thee from evil, and
evil from thee.

(Compare

Job 28:28).

getting--or possession; a desire for wisdom is wise.

As you highly esteem her, she will raise you to honor.

embrace her--with fond affection.

ornament--such as the chaplet or wreath of conquerors.

deliver--(Compare

Ge 14:20).

The allusion to a shield, contained in the Hebrew, suggests
protection as well as honor (compare

Pr 4:6).

primaryText.PRO:4:10: Listen, my son, and receive my sayings. The years of your life will be many.
primaryText.PRO:4:11: I have taught you in the way of wisdom. I have led you in straight paths.
primaryText.PRO:4:12: When you go, your steps will not be hampered. When you run, you will not stumble.
primaryText.PRO:4:13: Take firm hold of instruction. Don’t let her go. Keep her, for she is your life.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 2:1; 3:2).

way of wisdom--which it prescribes.

led thee--literally, "caused thee to tread," as a path

(Ps 107:7).

not be straitened--have ample room

(Ps 18:36).

(Compare

Pr 3:18).

The figure of laying hold with the hand suggests earnest effort.

primaryText.PRO:4:14: Don’t enter into the path of the wicked. Don’t walk in the way of evil men.
primaryText.PRO:4:15: Avoid it, and don’t pass by it. Turn from it, and pass on.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Ps 1:1).

Avoid all temptations to the beginning of evil.

primaryText.PRO:4:16: For they don’t sleep unless they do evil. Their sleep is taken away, unless they make someone fall.
primaryText.PRO:4:17: For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.

evidence.quote:
The reason is found in the character of sinners, whose zeal
to do evil is forcibly depicted

(Pr 6:4;
Ps 36:5).

They live by flagrant vices

(Pr 1:13).

Some prefer to render, "Their bread is wickedness, their drink
