violence" (compare

Job 15:16; 34:7).

primaryText.PRO:4:18: But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light that shines more and more until the perfect day.
primaryText.PRO:4:19: The way of the wicked is like darkness. They don’t know what they stumble over.

evidence.quote:
As shining light increases from twilight to noonday splendor,
so the course of the just increases in purity, but that of the wicked is
as thickest darkness, in which one knows not on what he stumbles.

primaryText.PRO:4:20: My son, attend to my words. Turn your ear to my sayings.
primaryText.PRO:4:21: Let them not depart from your eyes. Keep them in the center of your heart.
primaryText.PRO:4:22: For they are life to those who find them, and health to their whole body.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 4:10, 13;
Pr 3:8,

&c.).

health . . . flesh--by preserving from vices
destructive of health.

primaryText.PRO:4:23: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

evidence.quote:
with all diligence--or, "above," or "more than all,"
custody (compare Margin), all that is kept (compare

Eze 38:7),

because the heart is the depository of all wisdom and the source of
whatever affects life and character

(Mt 12:35; 15:19).

primaryText.PRO:4:24: Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you.

evidence.quote:
a froward mouth--that is, a mouth, or words of ill nature. The
Hebrew word differs from that used

(Pr 2:15; 3:32).

perverse--or, "quarreling."

lips--or, "words."

primaryText.PRO:4:25: Let your eyes look straight ahead. Fix your gaze directly before you.

evidence.quote:
Let . . . before thee--that is, pursue a sincere and direct
purpose, avoiding temptations.

primaryText.PRO:4:26: Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established.

evidence.quote: Ponder--Consider well; a wise course results from wise forethought.

primaryText.PRO:4:27: Don’t turn to the right hand nor to the left. Remove your foot from evil.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 4:25).

Avoid all by-paths of evil

(De 2:27; 17:11).

A life of integrity requires attention to heart, speech, eyes, and
conduct.

primaryText.PRO:5:1: My son, pay attention to my wisdom. Turn your ear to my understanding,
primaryText.PRO:5:2: that you may maintain discretion, that your lips may preserve knowledge.

evidence.quote:
This connection of wisdom and understanding is frequent

(Pr 2:2; 3:7);

the first denotes the use of wise means for wise ends; the other, the
exercise of a proper discrimination in their discovery.

regard--or, "observe."

keep--preserve constantly.

primaryText.PRO:5:3: For the lips of an adulteress drip honey. Her mouth is smoother than oil,
primaryText.PRO:5:4: but in the end she is as bitter as wormwood, and as sharp as a two-edged sword.
primaryText.PRO:5:5: Her feet go down to death. Her steps lead straight to Sheol.
primaryText.PRO:5:6: She gives no thought to the way of life. Her ways are crooked, and she doesn’t know it.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 2:16).

Her enticing promises are deceitful.

her end--literally, "her future," in sense of reward, what follows
(compare

Ps 37:37; 73:17).

Its nature is evinced by the use of figures, opposite those of

Pr 5:3.

The physical and moral suffering of the deluded profligate are
notoriously terrible.
feet . . . , steps--that is, course of life ends in death.

her ways . . . know--Some prefer, "that she may not ponder the path
of life," &c.; but perhaps a better sense is, "her ways are varied, so
as to prevent your knowledge of her true character, and so of true
happiness."

primaryText.PRO:5:10: lest strangers feast on your wealth, and your labors enrich another man’s house.
primaryText.PRO:5:7: Now therefore, my sons, listen to me. Don’t depart from the words of my mouth.
primaryText.PRO:5:8: Remove your way far from her. Don’t come near the door of her house,
primaryText.PRO:5:9: lest you give your honor to others, and your years to the cruel one;

evidence.quote: Avoid the slightest temptation.

thine honour--in whatever consisting, strength

(Pr 3:13)

or wealth.

thy years--by cutting them off in dissipation.

unto the cruel--for such the sensual are apt to become.

wealth--literally, "strength," or the result of it.

labours--the fruit of thy painful exertions

(Ps 127:2).

There may be a reference to slavery, a commuted punishment for death
due the adulterer

(De 22:22).

primaryText.PRO:5:11: You will groan at your latter end, when your flesh and your body are consumed,
primaryText.PRO:5:12: and say, “How I have hated instruction, and my heart despised reproof.
primaryText.PRO:5:13: I haven’t obeyed the voice of my teachers, nor turned my ear to those who instructed me!
primaryText.PRO:5:14: I have come to the brink of utter ruin, among the gathered assembly.”

evidence.quote:
at the last--the end, or reward (compare

Pr 5:4).

mourn--roar in pain.

flesh and . . . body--the whole person under incurable disease.

The ruined sinner vainly laments his neglect of warning and his
sad fate in being brought to public disgrace.

evil--for affliction, as in

Ge 19:20; 49:15.

primaryText.PRO:5:15: Drink water out of your own cistern, running water out of your own well.
primaryText.PRO:5:16: Should your springs overflow in the streets, streams of water in the public squares?
primaryText.PRO:5:17: Let them be for yourself alone, not for strangers with you.

evidence.quote:
By figures, in which well, cistern, and fountain

[Pr 5:15, 18]

represent the wife, and rivers of waters

[Pr 5:16]

the children, men are exhorted to constancy and satisfaction in lawful
conjugal enjoyments. In

Pr 5:16,

fountains (in the plural) rather denote the produce or waters of
a spring, literally, "what is from a spring," and corresponds with
"rivers of waters."
only thine own--harlots' children have no known father.

primaryText.PRO:5:18: Let your spring be blessed. Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
primaryText.PRO:5:19: A loving doe and a graceful deer— let her breasts satisfy you at all times. Be captivated always with her love.
primaryText.PRO:5:20: For why should you, my son, be captivated with an adulteress? Why embrace the bosom of another?

evidence.quote:
By figures, in which well, cistern, and fountain

[Pr 5:15, 18]

represent the wife, and rivers of waters

[Pr 5:16]

the children, men are exhorted to constancy and satisfaction in lawful
conjugal enjoyments. In

Pr 5:16,

fountains (in the plural) rather denote the produce or waters of
a spring, literally, "what is from a spring," and corresponds with
"rivers of waters."
wife . . . youth--married in youth.

loving . . . roe--other figures for a wife from the well-known
beauty of these animals.

breasts--(Compare

So 1:13;
Eze 23:3, 8).

ravished--literally, "intoxicated," that is, fully satisfied.

primaryText.PRO:5:21: For the ways of man are before the LORD’s eyes. He examines all his paths.
primaryText.PRO:5:22: The evil deeds of the wicked ensnare him. The cords of his sin hold him firmly.

evidence.quote: The reason, God's eye is on you,
and He will cause sin to bring its punishment.

primaryText.PRO:5:23: He will die for lack of instruction. In the greatness of his folly, he will go astray.

evidence.quote: and He will cause sin to bring its punishment.

without instruction--literally, "in want of instruction," having
refused it (compare

Job 13:18;
Heb 11:24).

go astray--literally, "be drunken." The word "ravished"

(Pr 5:19)

here denotes fulness of punishment.

primaryText.PRO:6:1: My son, if you have become collateral for your neighbor, if you have struck your hands in pledge for a stranger,
primaryText.PRO:6:2: you are trapped by the words of your mouth; you are ensnared with the words of your mouth.
primaryText.PRO:6:3: Do this now, my son, and deliver yourself, since you have come into the hand of your neighbor. Go, humble yourself. Press your plea with your neighbor.
primaryText.PRO:6:4: Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids.
primaryText.PRO:6:5: Free yourself, like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the snare of the fowler.

evidence.quote:
if--The condition extends through both verses.

be surety--art pledged.

stricken . . . hand--bargained (compare

Job 17:3).

with a stranger--that is, for a friend (compare

Pr 11:15; 17:18).

come . . . friend--in his power.

humble . . . sure thy friend--urge as a suppliant; that is, induce the
friend to provide otherwise for his debt, or secure the surety.
The danger requires promptness.

primaryText.PRO:6:6: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise;
primaryText.PRO:6:7: which having no chief, overseer, or ruler,
primaryText.PRO:6:8: provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest.

evidence.quote:
The improvident sluggards usually want sureties. Hence, such are
advised to industry by the ant's example.

primaryText.PRO:6:10: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep—
primaryText.PRO:6:11: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
primaryText.PRO:6:9: How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep?

evidence.quote: Their conduct graphically described;

and the fruits of their self-indulgence and indolence presented.

as . . . travelleth--literally, "one who walks
backwards and forwards," that is, a highwayman.

armed man--that is, one prepared to destroy.

primaryText.PRO:6:12: A worthless person, a man of iniquity, is he who walks with a perverse mouth,
primaryText.PRO:6:13: who winks with his eyes, who signals with his feet, who motions with his fingers,
primaryText.PRO:6:14: in whose heart is perverseness, who devises evil continually, who always sows discord.
primaryText.PRO:6:15: Therefore his calamity will come suddenly. He will be broken suddenly, and that without remedy.

evidence.quote:
A naughty person--literally, "A man of Belial," or of
worthlessness, that is, for good, and so depraved, or wicked (compare

1Sa 25:25; 30:22,

&c.). Idleness and vice are allied. Though indolent in acts, he
actively and habitually (walketh) is ill-natured in speech

(Pr 4:24).

If, for fear of detection, he does not speak, he uses signs
to carry on his intrigues. These signs are still so used in the East.

Frowardness--as in

Pr 2:14.

deviseth--literally, "constructs, as an artisan."

mischief--evil to others.

discord--especially litigation. Cunning is the talent of the weak and
lazy.

Suddenness aggravates evil (compare

Pr 6:11; 29:1).

calamity--literally, "a crushing weight."

broken--shivered as a potter's vessel; utterly destroyed

(Ps 2:9).

primaryText.PRO:6:16: There are six things which the LORD hates; yes, seven which are an abomination to him:
primaryText.PRO:6:17: arrogant eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood,
primaryText.PRO:6:18: a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that are swift in running to mischief,
primaryText.PRO:6:19: a false witness who utters lies, and he who sows discord among brothers.

evidence.quote:
proud look--literally, "eyes of loftiness"

(Ps 131:1).

Eyes, tongue, &c., for persons.

primaryText.PRO:6:20: My son, keep your father’s commandment, and don’t forsake your mother’s teaching.
primaryText.PRO:6:21: Bind them continually on your heart. Tie them around your neck.
primaryText.PRO:6:22: When you walk, it will lead you. When you sleep, it will watch over you. When you awake, it will talk with you.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 1:8; 3:3,

&c.).

primaryText.PRO:6:23: For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light. Reproofs of instruction are the way of life,
primaryText.PRO:6:24: to keep you from the immoral woman, from the flattery of the wayward wife’s tongue.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 1:8; 3:3,

&c.).

reproofs--

(Pr 1:23)

the convictions of error produced by instruction.

A specimen of its benefit. By appreciating truth, men are not
affected by lying flattery.

primaryText.PRO:6:25: Don’t lust after her beauty in your heart, neither let her captivate you with her eyelids.
primaryText.PRO:6:26: For a prostitute reduces you to a piece of bread. The adulteress hunts for your precious life.

evidence.quote:
One of the cautions of this instruction, avoid alluring beauty.

take--or, "ensnare."

eyelids--By painting the lashes, women enhanced beauty.

The supplied words give a better sense than the old version: "The
price of a whore is a piece of bread."

adulteress--(Compare Margin), which the parallel and context

(Pr 6:29-35)

sustain. Of similar results of this sin, compare

Pr 5:9-12.

will hunt--alluding to the snares spread by harlots (compare

Pr 7:6-8).

precious life--more valuable than all else.

primaryText.PRO:6:27: Can a man scoop fire into his lap, and his clothes not be burned?
primaryText.PRO:6:28: Or can one walk on hot coals, and his feet not be scorched?
primaryText.PRO:6:29: So is he who goes in to his neighbor’s wife. Whoever touches her will not be unpunished.

evidence.quote: The guilt and danger most obvious.

primaryText.PRO:6:30: Men don’t despise a thief if he steals to satisfy himself when he is hungry,
primaryText.PRO:6:31: but if he is found, he shall restore seven times. He shall give all the wealth of his house.

evidence.quote: Such a thief is pitied, though heavily punished.

sevenfold--(compare

Ex 22:1-4),

for many, ample (compare

Ge 4:24;
Mt 18:21),

even if all his wealth is taken.

primaryText.PRO:6:32: He who commits adultery with a woman is void of understanding. He who does it destroys his own soul.
primaryText.PRO:6:33: He will get wounds and dishonor. His reproach will not be wiped away.

evidence.quote:
lacketh understanding--or, "heart"; destitute of moral principle
and prudence.

primaryText.PRO:6:34: For jealousy arouses the fury of the husband. He won’t spare in the day of vengeance.
primaryText.PRO:6:35: He won’t regard any ransom, neither will he rest content, though you give many gifts.

evidence.quote:
nor any terms of reconciliation be admitted.

regard--or, "accept" any ransom.

primaryText.PRO:7:1: My son, keep my words. Lay up my commandments within you.
primaryText.PRO:7:2: Keep my commandments and live! Guard my teaching as the apple of your eye.
primaryText.PRO:7:3: Bind them on your fingers. Write them on the tablet of your heart.
primaryText.PRO:7:4: Tell wisdom, “You are my sister.” Call understanding your relative,
primaryText.PRO:7:5: that they may keep you from the strange woman, from the foreigner who flatters with her words.

evidence.quote:
Similar calls

(Pr 3:1-3; 4:10,

&c.).

apple . . . eye--pupil of eye, a custody

(Pr 4:23)

of special value.
Bind . . . fingers--as inscriptions on rings.

The design of the teaching (compare

Pr 2:16; 6:24).

primaryText.PRO:7:6: For at the window of my house, I looked out through my lattice.
primaryText.PRO:7:7: I saw among the simple ones. I discerned among the youths a young man void of understanding,
primaryText.PRO:7:8: passing through the street near her corner, he went the way to her house,
primaryText.PRO:7:9: in the twilight, in the evening of the day, in the middle of the night and in the darkness.

evidence.quote:
For--or, "Since," introducing an example to illustrate the warning,
which, whether a narrative or a parable, is equally pertinent.

window--or, "opening"

looked--literally, "watched earnestly"

(Jud 5:28).

casement--or, "lattice."

simple--as in

Pr 1:4.

void of, &c.--(Compare

Pr 6:32).

her corner--where she was usually found.

went . . . house--implying, perhaps, confidence in himself by his
manner, as denoted in the word

went--literally, "tread pompously."

The time, twilight, ending in darkness.

black . . . night--literally, "pupil," or, "eye," that is, middle of
night.

primaryText.PRO:7:10: Behold, there a woman met him with the attire of a prostitute, and with crafty intent.
primaryText.PRO:7:11: She is loud and defiant. Her feet don’t stay in her house.
primaryText.PRO:7:12: Now she is in the streets, now in the squares, and lurking at every corner.

evidence.quote:
attire--that of harlots was sometimes peculiar.

subtile--or, "wary," "cunning."

loud--or, "noisy," "bustling."

stubborn--not submissive.

without . . . streets, . . . corner--(Compare

1Ti 5:13;
Tit 2:5).

primaryText.PRO:7:13: So she caught him, and kissed him. With an impudent face she said to him:
primaryText.PRO:7:14: “Sacrifices of peace offerings are with me. Today I have paid my vows.
primaryText.PRO:7:15: Therefore I came out to meet you, to diligently seek your face, and I have found you.

evidence.quote:
The preparations for a feast do not necessarily imply peculiar
religious professions. The offerer retained part of the victim for a
feast

(Le 3:9,

&c.). This feast she professes was prepared for him whom she boldly
addresses as one sought specially to partake of it.

primaryText.PRO:7:16: I have spread my couch with carpets of tapestry, with striped cloths of the yarn of Egypt.
primaryText.PRO:7:17: I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.

evidence.quote: my bed--or, "couch," adorned in the costliest manner.
bed--a place for sleeping.

primaryText.PRO:7:18: Come, let’s take our fill of loving until the morning. Let’s solace ourselves with loving.
primaryText.PRO:7:19: For my husband isn’t at home. He has gone on a long journey.
primaryText.PRO:7:20: He has taken a bag of money with him. He will come home at the full moon.”
primaryText.PRO:7:21: With persuasive words, she led him astray. With the flattering of her lips, she seduced him.
primaryText.PRO:7:22: He followed her immediately, as an ox goes to the slaughter, as a fool stepping into a noose.
primaryText.PRO:7:23: Until an arrow strikes through his liver, as a bird hurries to the snare, and doesn’t know that it will cost his life.

evidence.quote: There is no fear of discovery.

the day appointed--perhaps, literally, "a full moon," that is, a
fortnight's time (compare

Pr 7:19).

caused . . . yield--or, "inclines."

flattering--(Compare

Pr 5:3).

forced him--by persuasion overcoming his scruples.

straightway--quickly, either as ignorant of danger, or incapable of
resistance.

Till--He is now caught

(Pr 6:26).

primaryText.PRO:7:24: Now therefore, sons, listen to me. Pay attention to the words of my mouth.
primaryText.PRO:7:25: Don’t let your heart turn to her ways. Don’t go astray in her paths,

evidence.quote:
The inferential admonition is followed

(Pr 7:26, 27),

by a more general allegation of the evils of this vice.

primaryText.PRO:7:26: for she has thrown down many wounded. Yes, all her slain are a mighty army.
primaryText.PRO:7:27: Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the rooms of death.

evidence.quote: Even the mightiest fail to resist her deathly allurements.

primaryText.PRO:8:1: Doesn’t wisdom cry out? Doesn’t understanding raise her voice?
primaryText.PRO:8:2: On the top of high places by the way, where the paths meet, she stands.
primaryText.PRO:8:3: Beside the gates, at the entry of the city, at the entry doors, she cries aloud:
primaryText.PRO:8:4: “I call to you men! I send my voice to the sons of mankind.

evidence.quote:
The publicity and universality of the call contrast with the
secrecy and intrigues of the wicked

(Pr 7:8,

&c.).

primaryText.PRO:8:5: You simple, understand prudence! You fools, be of an understanding heart!
primaryText.PRO:8:6: Hear, for I will speak excellent things. The opening of my lips is for right things.
primaryText.PRO:8:7: For my mouth speaks truth. Wickedness is an abomination to my lips.
primaryText.PRO:8:8: All the words of my mouth are in righteousness. There is nothing crooked or perverse in them.
primaryText.PRO:8:9: They are all plain to him who understands, right to those who find knowledge.

evidence.quote:
wisdom--literally, "subtilty" in a good sense, or, "prudence."

fools--as

Pr 1:22.

excellent things--or, "plain," "manifest."

opening . . . things--upright words.

For . . . truth--literally, "My palate shall meditate," or (as
Orientals did) "mutter," my thoughts expressed only to myself are truth.

wickedness--specially falsehood, as opposed to truth.

in righteousness--or, "righteous"

(Ps 9:8:11:7).

froward--literally, "twisted," or contradictory, that is, to truth.

plain . . . understandeth--easily seen by those who apply their
minds.

that find--implying search.

primaryText.PRO:8:10: Receive my instruction rather than silver, knowledge rather than choice gold.
primaryText.PRO:8:11: For wisdom is better than rubies. All the things that may be desired can’t be compared to it.
primaryText.PRO:8:12: “I, wisdom, have made prudence my dwelling. Find out knowledge and discretion.
primaryText.PRO:8:13: The fear of the LORD is to hate evil. I hate pride, arrogance, the evil way, and the perverse mouth.

evidence.quote: not silver--preferable to it, so last clause implies comparison.

(Compare

Pr 3:14, 15).

prudence--as in

Pr 8:5.

The connection of "wisdom" and "prudence" is that of the dictates of
sound wisdom and its application.

find . . . inventions--or, "devices," "discreet ways"

(Pr 1:4).

For such is the effect of the fear of God, by which hatred to evil
preserves from it.

froward mouth--or, "speech"

(Pr 2:12; 6:14).

primaryText.PRO:8:14: Counsel and sound knowledge are mine. I have understanding and power.
primaryText.PRO:8:15: By me kings reign, and princes decree justice.
primaryText.PRO:8:16: By me princes rule, nobles, and all the righteous rulers of the earth.
primaryText.PRO:8:17: I love those who love me. Those who seek me diligently will find me.

evidence.quote:
It also gives the elements of good character in counsel.

sound wisdom--

(Pr 2:7).

I . . . strength--or, "As for me, understanding is strength to me,"
the source of power

(Ec 9:16);

good judgment gives more efficiency to actions;
of which a wisely conducted government is an example.

early--or, "diligently," which may include the usual sense of early
in life.

primaryText.PRO:8:18: With me are riches, honor, enduring wealth, and prosperity.
primaryText.PRO:8:19: My fruit is better than gold, yes, than fine gold, my yield than choice silver.
primaryText.PRO:8:20: I walk in the way of righteousness, in the middle of the paths of justice,
primaryText.PRO:8:21: that I may give wealth to those who love me. I fill their treasuries.

evidence.quote:
durable riches . . . righteousness--Such are the "riches," enduring
sources of happiness in moral possessions (compare

Pr 3:16).

(Compare

Pr 8:11; 3:16).

The courses in which wisdom leads conduct to a true present
prosperity

(Pr 23:5).

primaryText.PRO:8:22: “The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old.
primaryText.PRO:8:23: I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed.
primaryText.PRO:8:24: When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water.
primaryText.PRO:8:25: Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born;
primaryText.PRO:8:26: while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world.

evidence.quote:
Strictly, God's attributes are part of Himself. Yet, to the
poetical structure of the whole passage, this commendation of wisdom is
entirely consonant. In order of time all His attributes are coincident
and eternal as Himself. But to set forth the importance of wisdom as
devising the products of benevolence and power, it is here assigned a
precedence. As it has such in divine, so should it be desired in human,
affairs (compare

Pr 3:19).

possessed--or, "created"; in either sense, the idea of precedence.

in the beginning--or simply, "beginning," in apposition with "me."

before . . . of old--preceding the most ancient deeds.

I was set up--ordained, or inaugurated

(Ps 2:6).

The other terms carry out the idea of the earliest antiquity, and
illustrate it by the details of creation

[Pr 8:24-29].

brought forth--(Compare

Ps 90:2).

abounding--or, "laden with water."
settled--that is, sunk in foundations.

fields--or, "out places," "deserts," as opposite to (habitable)
"world."

highest part--or, "sum," all particles together,

primaryText.PRO:8:27: When he established the heavens, I was there. When he set a circle on the surface of the deep,
primaryText.PRO:8:28: when he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong,
primaryText.PRO:8:29: when he gave to the sea its boundary, that the waters should not violate his commandment, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,

evidence.quote:
Strictly, God's attributes are part of Himself. Yet, to the
poetical structure of the whole passage, this commendation of wisdom is
entirely consonant. In order of time all His attributes are coincident
and eternal as Himself. But to set forth the importance of wisdom as
devising the products of benevolence and power, it is here assigned a
precedence. As it has such in divine, so should it be desired in human,
affairs (compare

Pr 3:19).

possessed--or, "created"; in either sense, the idea of precedence.

in the beginning--or simply, "beginning," in apposition with "me."

before . . . of old--preceding the most ancient deeds.

when he set . . . depth--marked out the circle, according to the
popular idea of the earth, as circular, surrounded by depths on which
the visible concave heavens rested.

established . . . deep--that is, so as to sustain the waters above
and repress those below the firmament

(Ge 1:7-11;
Job 26:8).

commandment--better, the shore, that is, of the sea.

foundations--figuratively denotes the solid structure

(Job 38:4;
Ps 24:2).

primaryText.PRO:8:30: then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him,
primaryText.PRO:8:31: rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.

evidence.quote:
Strictly, God's attributes are part of Himself. Yet, to the
poetical structure of the whole passage, this commendation of wisdom is
entirely consonant. In order of time all His attributes are coincident
and eternal as Himself. But to set forth the importance of wisdom as
devising the products of benevolence and power, it is here assigned a
precedence. As it has such in divine, so should it be desired in human,
affairs (compare

Pr 3:19).

possessed--or, "created"; in either sense, the idea of precedence.

in the beginning--or simply, "beginning," in apposition with "me."

before . . . of old--preceding the most ancient deeds.

one brought up--an object of special and pleasing regard. The
bestowal of wisdom on men is represented by its finding a delightful
residence and pleasing God.

primaryText.PRO:8:32: “Now therefore, my sons, listen to me, for blessed are those who keep my ways.
primaryText.PRO:8:33: Hear instruction, and be wise. Don’t refuse it.
primaryText.PRO:8:34: Blessed is the man who hears me, watching daily at my gates, waiting at my door posts.
primaryText.PRO:8:35: For whoever finds me finds life, and will obtain favor from the LORD.

evidence.quote: Such an attribute men are urged to seek.

watching . . . waiting--literally, "so as to watch"; wait, denoting
a most sedulous attention.

(Compare

Lu 13:23, 24).

primaryText.PRO:8:36: But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul. All those who hate me love death.”

evidence.quote: Such an attribute men are urged to seek.

sinneth . . . me--or better, "missing me," as opposed to "finding"

[Pr 8:35].

love death--act as if they did (compare

Pr 17:9).

primaryText.PRO:9:1: Wisdom has built her house. She has carved out her seven pillars.
primaryText.PRO:9:2: She has prepared her meat. She has mixed her wine. She has also set her table.
primaryText.PRO:9:3: She has sent out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city:

evidence.quote:
house--(compare

Pr 8:34).

her--or, "its" (the house).

seven pillars--the number seven for many, or a sufficiency

(Pr 6:31).

mingled--to enhance the flavor

(Pr 23:30;
Isa 5:22).

furnished--literally, "set out," "arranged."

maidens--servants to invite (compare

Ps 68:11;
Isa 40:9).

highest places--ridges of heights, conspicuous places.

primaryText.PRO:9:4: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him,
primaryText.PRO:9:5: “Come, eat some of my bread, Drink some of the wine which I have mixed!
primaryText.PRO:9:6: Leave your simple ways, and live. Walk in the way of understanding.”

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 1:4; 6:32).

Wisdom not only supplies right but forbids wrong principles.

primaryText.PRO:9:7: One who corrects a mocker invites insult. One who reproves a wicked man invites abuse.
primaryText.PRO:9:8: Don’t reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you. Reprove a wise person, and he will love you.
primaryText.PRO:9:9: Instruct a wise person, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous person, and he will increase in learning.

evidence.quote:
shame--(Compare

Pr 3:35).

a blot--or, "stain on character." Both terms denote the evil done by
others to one whose faithfulness secures a wise man's love.
The more a wise man learns, the more he loves wisdom.

primaryText.PRO:9:10: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. The knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
primaryText.PRO:9:11: For by me your days will be multiplied. The years of your life will be increased.
primaryText.PRO:9:12: If you are wise, you are wise for yourself. If you mock, you alone will bear it.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 1:7).

of the holy--literally, "holies," persons or things, or both. This
knowledge gives right perception.
You are mainly concerned in your own conduct.

primaryText.PRO:9:13: The foolish woman is loud, undisciplined, and knows nothing.
primaryText.PRO:9:14: She sits at the door of her house, on a seat in the high places of the city,

evidence.quote:
foolish woman--or literally, "woman of folly," specially manifested
by such as are described.

clamorous--or, "noisy"

(Pr 7:11).

knoweth nothing--literally, "knoweth not what," that is, is right and
proper.

on a seat--literally, "throne," takes a prominent place, impudently
and haughtily.

primaryText.PRO:9:15: to call to those who pass by, who go straight on their ways,
primaryText.PRO:9:16: “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here.” As for him who is void of understanding, she says to him,

evidence.quote:
to allure those who are right-minded, and who are addressed
as in

Pr 9:4,

as

simple--that is, easily led

(Pr 1:4)

and unsettled, though willing to do right.

primaryText.PRO:9:17: “Stolen water is sweet. Food eaten in secret is pleasant.”

evidence.quote:
The language of a proverb, meaning that forbidden delights are
sweet and pleasant, as fruits of risk and danger.

primaryText.PRO:9:18: But he doesn’t know that the departed spirits are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.

primaryText.PRO:10:1: The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father; but a foolish son brings grief to his mother.
primaryText.PRO:10:2: Treasures of wickedness profit nothing, but righteousness delivers from death.
primaryText.PRO:10:3: The LORD will not allow the soul of the righteous to go hungry, but he thrusts away the desire of the wicked.
primaryText.PRO:10:4: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth.

evidence.quote:
wise [and] foolish--as they follow or reject the
precepts of wisdom.

maketh . . . father--or, "gladdens a father."

heaviness--or, "grief."

Treasures . . . nothing--that is, Ill-gotten gains give no true
happiness (compare

Pr 4:17;
Mt 6:19).

righteousness--especially beneficence

(Ps 112:9).

death--the greatest of all evils.

(Compare

Ps 37:16-20).

The last clause is better: "He will repel the greedy desires of the
wicked."

slack--literally, "deceitful," failing of its purpose (compare

Ho 7:16).

maketh rich--(compare

Pr 10:22).

primaryText.PRO:10:5: He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during the harvest is a son who causes shame.
primaryText.PRO:10:6: Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but violence covers the mouth of the wicked.
primaryText.PRO:10:7: The memory of the righteous is blessed, but the name of the wicked will rot.
primaryText.PRO:10:8: The wise in heart accept commandments, but a chattering fool will fall.

evidence.quote:
son--as

Pr 1:8, 10,

and often.

sleepeth--in indolence, and not for rest.

causeth shame--literally, "is base" (compare

Pr 14:35; 17:2).

Blessings--literally, "Praises." The last clause is better: "The
mouth of the wicked covereth (or concealeth) violence (or mischievous
devices)" to be executed in due time

(Ps 5:9; 10:7;
Ro 3:14),

and hence has no praises (compare

Pr 10:11).

blessed--literally, "for a blessing," or praise.

shall rot--literally, "be worm-eaten," useless and disgusting.

wise, &c.--(compare

Pr 9:8, 9, 16),

opposed to

prating fool--or, "fool of lips of wicked language."

fall--headlong, suddenly.

primaryText.PRO:10:10: One who winks with the eye causes sorrow, but a chattering fool will fall.
primaryText.PRO:10:11: The mouth of the righteous is a spring of life, but violence covers the mouth of the wicked.
primaryText.PRO:10:12: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs.
primaryText.PRO:10:9: He who walks blamelessly walks surely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.

evidence.quote:
perverteth his ways--acts deceitfully.

known--discovered and punished.

Two vices contrasted; hypocrisy, or insinuating evil against one

(Pr 6:13;
Ps 35:19),

and rashness of speech. In each case, the results are on the
evildoers.

a well--or, "source" of good to himself and others

(Joh 7:37, 38).

On last clause, see on

Pr 10:6.

strifes--or, "litigations."

covereth--by forgiveness and forbearance.

primaryText.PRO:10:13: Wisdom is found on the lips of him who has discernment, but a rod is for the back of him who is void of understanding.
primaryText.PRO:10:14: Wise men lay up knowledge, but the mouth of the foolish is near ruin.
primaryText.PRO:10:15: The rich man’s wealth is his strong city. The destruction of the poor is their poverty.
primaryText.PRO:10:16: The labor of the righteous leads to life. The increase of the wicked leads to sin.

evidence.quote:
In the lips . . . found--hence, not beaten, as the wicked-speaking
fool.

void of understanding--

(Pr 6:32; 7:7).

lay up knowledge--that is, as treasures for good use.

mouth . . . destruction--or, "as to the mouth," &c., destruction is
near; they expose themselves to evil by prating.

Both by trusting in "uncertain riches"

(1Ti 6:17),

or by the evils of poverty

(Pr 30:9),

men, not fearing God, fall into dangers.

The industry of the righteous is alone truly successful, while the
earnings of the wicked tempt and lead to sin.

primaryText.PRO:10:17: He is in the way of life who heeds correction, but he who forsakes reproof leads others astray.
primaryText.PRO:10:18: He who hides hatred has lying lips. He who utters a slander is a fool.
primaryText.PRO:10:19: In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.
primaryText.PRO:10:20: The tongue of the righteous is like choice silver. The heart of the wicked is of little worth.

evidence.quote:
keepeth--observes

(Pr 3:18; 4:22).

refuseth--or, "turns from reproof," which might direct him aright.

Both vices must one day be known and punished, and hence their
folly.

Much speech involves risk of sin; hence the wisdom of restraining
the tongue

(Ps 39:1;
Jas 1:26).

Right speech is the fruit of a good heart, but the wicked show
theirs to be useless.

primaryText.PRO:10:21: The lips of the righteous feed many, but the foolish die for lack of understanding.
primaryText.PRO:10:22: The LORD’s blessing brings wealth, and he adds no trouble to it.
primaryText.PRO:10:23: It is a fool’s pleasure to do wickedness, but wisdom is a man of understanding’s pleasure.
primaryText.PRO:10:24: What the wicked fear will overtake them, but the desire of the righteous will be granted.

evidence.quote:
Fools not only fail to benefit others, as do the righteous, but
procure their own ruin (compare

Pr 10:11, 17;
Ho 4:6).

it maketh, &c.--"it" is emphatic. Riches from God are without the
sorrow of ill-gotten wealth (compare

Ec 2:21-23;
1Ti 6:9, 10, 17).
Sin is the pleasure of the wicked; wisdom that of the good.

it--the very thing. The wicked get dreaded evil; the righteous,
desired good.

primaryText.PRO:10:25: When the whirlwind passes, the wicked is no more; but the righteous stand firm forever.
primaryText.PRO:10:26: As vinegar to the teeth, and as smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him.
primaryText.PRO:10:27: The fear of the LORD prolongs days, but the years of the wicked shall be shortened.
primaryText.PRO:10:28: The prospect of the righteous is joy, but the hope of the wicked will perish.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Ps 1:4; 37:9, 10, 36).

righteous . . . foundation--well laid and firm

(Mt 7:24, 25).
that is, causes vexation.

gladness--in confidence of realizing it.

expectation . . . perish--in disappointment.

primaryText.PRO:10:29: The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the upright, but it is a destruction to the workers of iniquity.
primaryText.PRO:10:30: The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land.
primaryText.PRO:10:31: The mouth of the righteous produces wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off.
primaryText.PRO:10:32: The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked is perverse.

evidence.quote:
The way, &c.--that is, God's providence sustains the righteous and
overthrows the wicked

(Ho 14:9).

(Compare

Pr 12:3;
Ps 37:9-11; 102:28).

earth--or, "land of promise."

bringeth forth--literally, "germinates" as a plant.

froward--(Compare

Pr 2:12, 14).

cut off--as an unproductive plant.

know--regard and provide for

(Ps 1:6).

frowardness--all kinds of deceit and ill-nature. The word is plural.

primaryText.PRO:11:1: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but accurate weights are his delight.
primaryText.PRO:11:2: When pride comes, then comes shame, but with humility comes wisdom.
primaryText.PRO:11:3: The integrity of the upright shall guide them, but the perverseness of the treacherous shall destroy them.

evidence.quote:
(Compare Margin). The Hebrews used stones for weights.

just--complete in measure.

Self-conceit is unteachable; the humble grow wise (compare

Pr 16:18; 18:12).

guide--to lead, as a shepherd

(Pr 6:7;
Ps 78:52).

perverseness--ill-nature.

destroy--with violence.

primaryText.PRO:11:4: Riches don’t profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death.
primaryText.PRO:11:5: The righteousness of the blameless will direct his way, but the wicked shall fall by his own wickedness.
primaryText.PRO:11:6: The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them, but the unfaithful will be trapped by evil desires.
primaryText.PRO:11:7: When a wicked man dies, hope perishes, and expectation of power comes to nothing.
primaryText.PRO:11:8: A righteous person is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked takes his place.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 10:2).

wrath--that is, of God.

direct--or, "make plain"; wicked ways are not plain

(Pr 13:17).

deliver them--that is, from evil, which the wicked suffer by their
own doings

(Pr 5:22;
Ps 9:16).

expectation . . . perish--for death cuts short all his plans

(Lu 16:25).

hope of unjust--better, "hope of wealth," or "power" (compare

Isa 40:29,

Hebrew). This gives an advance on the sentiment of the first
clause. Even hopes of gain die with him.

Perhaps the trouble prepared by the wicked, and which he
inherits (compare

Pr 11:6).

primaryText.PRO:11:10: When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices. When the wicked perish, there is shouting.
primaryText.PRO:11:11: By the blessing of the upright, the city is exalted, but it is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked.
primaryText.PRO:11:9: With his mouth the godless man destroys his neighbor, but the righteous will be delivered through knowledge.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Ps 35:16;
Da 11:32).

The just is saved by superior discernment.

The last may be a reason for the first. Together, they set
forth the relative moral worth of good and bad men.
By the blessing--implying active benevolence.

primaryText.PRO:11:12: One who despises his neighbor is void of wisdom, but a man of understanding holds his peace.
primaryText.PRO:11:13: One who brings gossip betrays a confidence, but one who is of a trustworthy spirit is one who keeps a secret.
primaryText.PRO:11:14: Where there is no wise guidance, the nation falls, but in the multitude of counselors there is victory.

evidence.quote:
despiseth--or, "reviles," a course contrasted with the prudent
silence of the wise.

holdeth his peace--as if neither hearing nor telling.

tale-bearer--(Compare Margin), one trading as a peddler in
scandal, whose propensity to talk leads him to betray confidence.

counsel--the art of governing

(Pr 1:5).

counsellors--literally, "one giving counsel"; the participle used as
a collective.

primaryText.PRO:11:15: He who is collateral for a stranger will suffer for it, but he who refuses pledges of collateral is secure.
primaryText.PRO:11:16: A gracious woman obtains honor, but violent men obtain riches.
primaryText.PRO:11:17: The merciful man does good to his own soul, but he who is cruel troubles his own flesh.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 6:1).

suretiship--(Compare Margin), the actors put for the action, which
may be lawfully hated.

retaineth--or literally, "lay hold of as a support." Honor is to a
feeble woman thus as valuable as riches to men.

merciful--kind to others; opposed to cruel. Such benefit themselves
by doing good to others (compare

Pr 24:5),

while the cruel injure themselves as well as others.

flesh--that is, his body, by penuriousness

(Col 2:23).

primaryText.PRO:11:18: Wicked people earn deceitful wages, but one who sows righteousness reaps a sure reward.
primaryText.PRO:11:19: He who is truly righteous gets life. He who pursues evil gets death.
primaryText.PRO:11:20: Those who are perverse in heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those whose ways are blameless are his delight.
primaryText.PRO:11:21: Most certainly, the evil man will not be unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered.

evidence.quote:
a deceitful work--or, "wages," which fail to satisfy, or flee away

(Pr 10:2; 23:5).

sure reward--or, "gain," as from trading

(Ho 10:12;
Ga 6:8, 9).

Inference from

Pr 11:18

(compare

Pr 11:5, 6; 10:16).

(Compare

Pr 11:5).

froward--as in

Pr 2:15,

opposed to the simplicity and purity of the upright.

in their way--or, "conduct."

The combined power of the wicked cannot free them from just
punishment, while the unaided children of the righteous find deliverance
by reason of their pious relationship

(Ps 37:25, 26).

primaryText.PRO:11:22: Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout, is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion.
primaryText.PRO:11:23: The desire of the righteous is only good. The expectation of the wicked is wrath.

evidence.quote:
Jewels were often suspended from the nose

(Ge 24:47;
Isa 3:21).

Thus adorned, a hog disgusts less than a fair and indiscreet woman.

(Compare

Pr 10:28).

wrath--is that of God.

primaryText.PRO:11:24: There is one who scatters, and increases yet more. There is one who withholds more than is appropriate, but gains poverty.
primaryText.PRO:11:25: The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.
primaryText.PRO:11:26: People curse someone who withholds grain, but blessing will be on the head of him who sells it.

evidence.quote:
The scope of the whole is a comment on

Pr 11:23.

Thus liberality, by God's blessing, secures increase, while
penuriousness, instead of expected gain, procures poverty.

Another example of the truth of

Pr 11:23;

the miser loses reputation, though he saves corn.

selleth it--that is, at a fair price.

primaryText.PRO:11:27: He who diligently seeks good seeks favor, but he who searches after evil, it shall come to him.
primaryText.PRO:11:28: He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.
primaryText.PRO:11:29: He who troubles his own house shall inherit the wind. The foolish shall be servant to the wise of heart.

evidence.quote:
The scope of the whole is a comment on

Pr 11:23.

Thus liberality, by God's blessing, secures increase, while
penuriousness, instead of expected gain, procures poverty.

good [and] mischief--that is, of others.

procureth . . . seeketh--implying success.

troubleth--as

Pr 15:27

explains, by greediness for gain (compare

Pr 11:17).

inherit . . . wind--Even successful, his gains are of no real value.
So the fool, thus acting, either comes to poverty, or heaps up for
others.

primaryText.PRO:11:30: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life. He who is wise wins souls.
primaryText.PRO:11:31: Behold, the righteous shall be repaid on the earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!

evidence.quote:
The scope of the whole is a comment on

Pr 11:23.

Thus liberality, by God's blessing, secures increase, while
penuriousness, instead of expected gain, procures poverty.

a tree of life--Blessings to others proceed from the works of the
righteous

(Pr 3:18).

winneth souls--(Compare Margin) to do them good as opposed to

Pr 6:25;
Eze 13:18

(compare

Lu 5:10).

Behold--Thus calling attention to the illustrations (compare

Pr 11:23),

the sentiment of which is confirmed even in time, not excluding future
rewards and punishments.

primaryText.PRO:12:1: Whoever loves correction loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.
primaryText.PRO:12:2: A good man shall obtain favor from the LORD, but he will condemn a man of wicked plans.
primaryText.PRO:12:3: A man shall not be established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous shall not be moved.
primaryText.PRO:12:4: A worthy woman is the crown of her husband, but a disgraceful wife is as rottenness in his bones.

evidence.quote:
loveth knowledge--as the fruit of instruction or training

(Pr 1:2).

hateth reproof--

(Pr 10:17).

brutish--stupid, regardless of his own welfare

(Ps 49:10; 73:22).

Wickedness cannot give permanent prosperity.

root . . . not be moved--firm as a flourishing
tree--

(Ps 1:3; 15:5;
Jer 17:8).

A virtuous woman--in the wide sense of well-disposed to all moral
duties

(Pr 31:10).

maketh ashamed--that is, by misconduct.

rottenness--an incurable evil.

primaryText.PRO:12:5: The thoughts of the righteous are just, but the advice of the wicked is deceitful.
primaryText.PRO:12:6: The words of the wicked are about lying in wait for blood, but the speech of the upright rescues them.
primaryText.PRO:12:7: The wicked are overthrown, and are no more, but the house of the righteous shall stand.
primaryText.PRO:12:8: A man shall be commended according to his wisdom, but he who has a warped mind shall be despised.

evidence.quote:
thoughts--or, "purposes."

are right--literally, "are judgment," that is, true decisions.

counsels--(Compare

Pr 11:14).

deceit--contrary to truth and honesty.

The words--or, "expressed designs" of the wicked are for evil
purposes.

the mouth--or, "words" of the righteous delivering instead of ensnaring
men.

Such conduct brings a proper return, by the destruction of the
wicked and well-being of the righteous and his family.

despised--as opposed to commended

(Pr 11:12).

perverse heart--or, "wicked principles," as opposed to one of wisdom.

primaryText.PRO:12:10: A righteous man respects the life of his animal, but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
primaryText.PRO:12:11: He who tills his land shall have plenty of bread, but he who chases fantasies is void of understanding.
primaryText.PRO:12:12: The wicked desires the plunder of evil men, but the root of the righteous flourishes.
primaryText.PRO:12:9: Better is he who is little known, and has a servant, than he who honors himself and lacks bread.

evidence.quote:
despised--held in little repute, obscure

(1Sa 18:23;
Isa 3:5).

hath a servant--implying some means of honest living.

honoureth himself--is self-conceited.

regardeth--literally, "knoweth"

(Ps 1:6).

mercies . . . cruel--as acts of compassion ungraciously rendered to the
needy. The righteous more regards a beast than the wicked a man.

The idler's fate is the result of indolence and want of principle

(Pr 6:32; 7:7).

the wicked . . . evil--They love the crafty arts of deception.

the root . . . fruit--their own resources supply them; or, it may be
rendered: "He (God) giveth, or, sets

(Eze 17:22)

the root of the righteous," and hence it is firm: or, the verb is
impersonal; "As to the root . . . it is firm"

(Pr 17:19).

primaryText.PRO:12:13: An evil man is trapped by sinfulness of lips, but the righteous shall come out of trouble.
primaryText.PRO:12:14: A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth. The work of a man’s hands shall be rewarded to him.
primaryText.PRO:12:15: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but he who is wise listens to counsel.
primaryText.PRO:12:16: A fool shows his annoyance the same day, but one who overlooks an insult is prudent.

evidence.quote:
The wicked is snared, &c.--The sentiment expanded. While the
wicked, such as liars, flatterers, &c., fall by their own words, the
righteous are unhurt. Their good conduct makes friends, and God rewards
them.

prudent . . . shame--He is slow to denounce his insulters

(Jas 1:19).

primaryText.PRO:12:17: He who is truthful testifies honestly, but a false witness lies.
primaryText.PRO:12:18: There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals.
primaryText.PRO:12:19: Truth’s lips will be established forever, but a lying tongue is only momentary.
primaryText.PRO:12:20: Deceit is in the heart of those who plot evil, but joy comes to the promoters of peace.

evidence.quote:
speaketh--literally, "speaketh hastily," or indiscreetly

(Ps 106:33),

as an angry man retorts harsh and provoking invectives.

tongue . . . health--by soothing and gentle language.

Words of truth are consistent, and stand all tests, while lies are
soon discovered and exposed.

that imagine--or, "plan"

(Pr 3:29).

They design a deceitful course, to which, with all its evils and
dangers to others and themselves, the happiness of peace-makers is
opposed (compare

Mt 5:9;
Ro 12:18).

primaryText.PRO:12:21: No mischief shall happen to the righteous, but the wicked shall be filled with evil.
primaryText.PRO:12:22: Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who do the truth are his delight.
primaryText.PRO:12:23: A prudent man keeps his knowledge, but the hearts of fools proclaim foolishness.
primaryText.PRO:12:24: The hands of the diligent ones shall rule, but laziness ends in slave labor.

evidence.quote:
no evil--(as in

Ps 91:10),

under God's wise limitations

(Ro 8:28).

mischief--as penal evil.

deal truly--or, "faithfully," that is, according to promises
(compare

Joh 3:21).

concealeth--by his modesty

(Pr 10:14; 11:13).

heart . . . proclaimeth--as his lips speak his
thoughts (compare

Ec 10:3).

slothful--(Compare Margin), so called because he fails to meet
his promises.

under tribute--not denoting legal taxes, but the obligation of
dependence.

primaryText.PRO:12:25: Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs it down, but a kind word makes it glad.
primaryText.PRO:12:26: A righteous person is cautious in friendship, but the way of the wicked leads them astray.
primaryText.PRO:12:27: The slothful man doesn’t roast his game, but the possessions of diligent men are prized.

evidence.quote: a good word--one of comfort.

more excellent--(Compare Margin); or, "more successful,"
while the wicked fail; or, we may read it: "The righteous guides his
friend, but," &c., that is, The ability of the righteous to aid others
is contrasted with the ruin to which the way of the wicked leads
themselves.

(Compare

Pr 12:24).

took in hunting--or, "his venison." He does not improve his advantages.

the substance . . . precious--or, "the wealth of a man of honor is
being diligent," or "diligence."

precious--literally, "honor"

(Ec 10:1).

primaryText.PRO:12:28: In the way of righteousness is life; in its path there is no death.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 8:8, 20,

&c.). A sentiment often stated; here first affirmatively, then
negatively.

primaryText.PRO:13:1: A wise son listens to his father’s instruction, but a scoffer doesn’t listen to rebuke.
primaryText.PRO:13:2: By the fruit of his lips, a man enjoys good things, but the unfaithful crave violence.
primaryText.PRO:13:3: He who guards his mouth guards his soul. One who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.
primaryText.PRO:13:4: The soul of the sluggard desires, and has nothing, but the desire of the diligent shall be fully satisfied.

evidence.quote:
shall eat--that is, obtain

(Pr 12:14).

transgressors--as in

Pr 2:22.

violence--or, "mischief" to themselves.

He . . . mouth . . . life--because evil speeches may provoke
violence from others.

he that openeth wide his lips shall have destruction--On last clause,
compare

Pr 10:14.

(Compare

Pr 12:11, 27).

primaryText.PRO:13:5: A righteous man hates lies, but a wicked man brings shame and disgrace.
primaryText.PRO:13:6: Righteousness guards the way of integrity, but wickedness overthrows the sinner.
primaryText.PRO:13:7: There are some who pretend to be rich, yet have nothing. There are some who pretend to be poor, yet have great wealth.
primaryText.PRO:13:8: The ransom of a man’s life is his riches, but the poor hear no threats.

evidence.quote:
loathsome . . . shame--better, causeth shame and reproach (compare

Pr 19:26),

by slander, &c., which the righteous hates.

A sentiment of frequent recurrence, that piety benefits and sin
injures.
In opposite ways men act hypocritically for gain of honor or wealth.

Riches save some from punishment, while others suffer because they
will not heed the rebuke of sloth, which makes and keeps them poor.

primaryText.PRO:13:10: Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice.
primaryText.PRO:13:11: Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles away, but he who gathers by hand makes it grow.
primaryText.PRO:13:12: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but when longing is fulfilled, it is a tree of life.
primaryText.PRO:13:9: The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is snuffed out.

evidence.quote:
light . . . lamp--prosperity; the first, the greater, and it

rejoiceth--burns brightly, or continues, while the other, at best
small, soon fails.

The obstinacy which attends self-conceit, produces contention,
which the well-advised, thus evincing modesty, avoid.

by vanity--or, "nothingness," that is, which is vain or useless
to the public (as card playing or similar vices).

gathereth . . . labour--(Compare Margin), little by little,
laboriously.

desire cometh--is realized.

a tree of life--or, "cause of happiness."

primaryText.PRO:13:13: Whoever despises instruction will pay for it, but he who respects a command will be rewarded.
primaryText.PRO:13:14: The teaching of the wise is a spring of life, to turn from the snares of death.
primaryText.PRO:13:15: Good understanding wins favor, but the way of the unfaithful is hard.
primaryText.PRO:13:16: Every prudent man acts from knowledge, but a fool exposes folly.

evidence.quote:
the word--that is, of advice, or, instruction (compare

Pr 10:27; 11:31).

(Compare

Pr 10:11).

fountain--or, "source of life."

to depart--(compare

Pr 1:2-4),

or, "for departing," &c., and so gives life.

Right perception and action secure good will, while evil ways
are difficult as a stony road. The wicked left of God find punishment of
sin in sinning.

hard--or, "harsh" (compare Hebrew:

De 21:4;
Jer 5:15).

dealeth--acts with foresight.

a fool . . . folly--for want of caution.

primaryText.PRO:13:17: A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a trustworthy envoy gains healing.
primaryText.PRO:13:18: Poverty and shame come to him who refuses discipline, but he who heeds correction shall be honored.
primaryText.PRO:13:19: Longing fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but fools detest turning from evil.
primaryText.PRO:13:20: One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm.

evidence.quote:
A wicked--or, "unfaithful"

messenger falleth into mischief--or, "by mischief," or "evil," and
so his errand fails. Contrasted is the character of the faithful, whose
faithfulness benefits others.

(Compare

Pr 10:17; 12:1).
Self-denial, which fools will not endure, is essential to success.
The benefits of good and evil of bad society are contrasted.

primaryText.PRO:13:21: Misfortune pursues sinners, but prosperity rewards the righteous.
primaryText.PRO:13:22: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the wealth of the sinner is stored for the righteous.
primaryText.PRO:13:23: An abundance of food is in poor people’s fields, but injustice sweeps it away.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 11:31).

good . . . repaid--or, "He (God) will repay good."

wealth . . . just--While good men's estates remain in their
families, God so orders that the gains of sinners enure to the just
(compare

Pr 28:8;
Ps 37:18, 22, 26,

&c.).

The laboring poor prosper more than those who injudiciously or
wickedly strive, by fraud and violence, to supersede the necessity of
lawful labor.

primaryText.PRO:13:24: One who spares the rod hates his son, but one who loves him is careful to discipline him.
primaryText.PRO:13:25: The righteous one eats to the satisfying of his soul, but the belly of the wicked goes hungry.

evidence.quote:
spareth--or, "withholds."

rod--of correction.

hateth--or, acts as if he hated him (compare

Pr 3:12; 8:36).

chasteneth . . . betimes--or, "diligently seeks for him all useful
discipline."

The comparative temporal prosperity of the righteous and wicked,
rather than contentment and discontent, is noted.

primaryText.PRO:14:1: Every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands.
primaryText.PRO:14:2: He who walks in his uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is perverse in his ways despises him.
primaryText.PRO:14:3: The fool’s talk brings a rod to his back, but the lips of the wise protect them.
primaryText.PRO:14:4: Where no oxen are, the crib is clean, but much increase is by the strength of the ox.
primaryText.PRO:14:5: A truthful witness will not lie, but a false witness pours out lies.

evidence.quote:
Every wise, &c.--literally, "The wisdoms" (compare

Pr 9:1)

"of women," plural, a distributive form of speech.

buildeth . . . house--increases wealth, which the foolish, by
mismanagement, lessen.

uprightness--is the fruit of fearing God, as falsehood and
ill-nature

(Pr 2:15; 3:32)

of despising Him and His law.

rod of pride--that is, the punishment of pride, which they evince
by their words. The words of the wise procure good to them.

crib is clean--empty; so "cleanness of teeth" denotes want of food
(compare

Am 4:6).

Men get the proper fruit of their doings

(Ga 6:7).

A faithful witness, &c.--one tested to be such.

utter lies--or, "breathe out lies"--that is, habitually lies

(Pr 6:19;

compare

Ac 9:1).

Or the sense is, that habitual truthfulness, or lying, will be evinced
in witness-bearing.

primaryText.PRO:14:10: The heart knows its own bitterness and joy; he will not share these with a stranger.
primaryText.PRO:14:6: A scoffer seeks wisdom, and doesn’t find it, but knowledge comes easily to a discerning person.
primaryText.PRO:14:7: Stay away from a foolish man, for you won’t find knowledge on his lips.
primaryText.PRO:14:8: The wisdom of the prudent is to think about his way, but the folly of fools is deceit.
primaryText.PRO:14:9: Fools mock at making atonement for sins, but among the upright there is good will.

evidence.quote: Avoid the society of those who cannot teach you.
Appearances deceive the thoughtless, but the prudent discriminate.

Fools make a mock at sin--or, "Sin deludes fools."

righteous . . . favour--that is, of God, instead of the punishment of
sin.
Each one best knows his own sorrows or joys.

primaryText.PRO:14:11: The house of the wicked will be overthrown, but the tent of the upright will flourish.
primaryText.PRO:14:12: There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.
primaryText.PRO:14:13: Even in laughter the heart may be sorrowful, and mirth may end in heaviness.
primaryText.PRO:14:14: The unfaithful will be repaid for his own ways; likewise a good man will be rewarded for his ways.
primaryText.PRO:14:15: A simple man believes everything, but the prudent man carefully considers his ways.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 12:7).

The contrast of the whole is enhanced by that of house and
tabernacle, a permanent and a temporary dwelling.

end thereof--or, "reward," what results (compare

Pr 5:4).

ways of death--leading to it.

The preceding sentiment illustrated by the disappointments of a
wicked or untimely joy.

filled . . . ways--receive retribution

(Pr 1:31).

a good man . . . himself--literally, "is away from such," will not
associate with him.

The simple . . . word--He is credulous, not from love, but
heedlessness

(Pr 13:16).

primaryText.PRO:14:16: A wise man fears and shuns evil, but the fool is hot headed and reckless.
primaryText.PRO:14:17: He who is quick to become angry will commit folly, and a crafty man is hated.
primaryText.PRO:14:18: The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
primaryText.PRO:14:19: The evil bow down before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous.
primaryText.PRO:14:20: The poor person is shunned even by his own neighbor, but the rich person has many friends.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 3:7; 28:14).

rageth--acts proudly and conceitedly.

He . . . angry--literally, "short of anger" (compare

Pr 14:29,

opposite idea).

man . . . hated--that is, the deliberate evildoer is more hated than
the rash.

inherit--as a portion (compare

Pr 3:35).

are crowned--literally, "are surrounded with it," abound in it.

Describes the humbling of the wicked by the punishment their sins
incur.

This sad but true picture of human nature is not given approvingly,
but only as a fact.

primaryText.PRO:14:21: He who despises his neighbor sins, but he who has pity on the poor is blessed.
primaryText.PRO:14:22: Don’t they go astray who plot evil? But love and faithfulness belong to those who plan good.
primaryText.PRO:14:23: In all hard work there is profit, but the talk of the lips leads only to poverty.
primaryText.PRO:14:24: The crown of the wise is their riches, but the folly of fools crowns them with folly.
primaryText.PRO:14:25: A truthful witness saves souls, but a false witness is deceitful.

evidence.quote:
For such contempt of the poor is contrasted as sinful with the
virtuous compassion of the good.

As usual, the interrogative negative strengthens the affirmative.

mercy and truth--that is, God's

(Ps 57:3; 61:7).

labour--painful diligence.

talk . . . penury--idle and vain promises and plans.

(Compare

Pr 3:16).

foolishness . . . folly--Folly remains, or produces folly; it has no
benefit.

Life often depends on truth-telling.

a deceitful . . . lies--He that breathes out lies is deceit, not to be
trusted

(Pr 14:5).

primaryText.PRO:14:26: In the fear of the LORD is a secure fortress, and he will be a refuge for his children.
primaryText.PRO:14:27: The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, turning people from the snares of death.
primaryText.PRO:14:28: In the multitude of people is the king’s glory, but in the lack of people is the destruction of the prince.
primaryText.PRO:14:29: He who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a quick temper displays folly.
primaryText.PRO:14:30: The life of the body is a heart at peace, but envy rots the bones.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 13:14).

fear of the Lord--or, "law of the wise," is wisdom

(Ps 111:10).
The teaching of a true political economy.

slow . . . understanding--(Compare

Pr 14:17).

hasty--(Compare

Pr 14:17).

exalteth folly--makes it conspicuous, as if delighting to honor it.

primaryText.PRO:14:31: He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors him.
primaryText.PRO:14:32: The wicked is brought down in his calamity, but in death, the righteous has a refuge.
primaryText.PRO:14:33: Wisdom rests in the heart of one who has understanding, and is even made known in the inward part of fools.
primaryText.PRO:14:34: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people.
primaryText.PRO:14:35: The king’s favor is toward a servant who deals wisely, but his wrath is toward one who causes shame.

evidence.quote:
driven--thrust out violently (compare

Ps 35:5, 6).

hath hope--trusteth

(Pr 10:2; 11:4;
Ps 2:12),

implying assurance of help.

resteth--preserved in quietness for use, while fools blazon their
folly

(Pr 12:23; 13:16).

Righteousness--just principles and actions.

exalteth--raises to honor.

is a reproach--brings on them the ill-will of others (compare

Pr 13:6).

wise--discreet or prudent.

causeth shame--

(Pr 10:5; 12:4)

acts basely.

primaryText.PRO:15:1: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
primaryText.PRO:15:2: The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
primaryText.PRO:15:3: The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
primaryText.PRO:15:4: A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.

evidence.quote:
soft--tender or gentle.

turneth . . . wrath--from any one.

stir up--as a smouldering fire is excited.

useth . . . aright--commends knowledge by its proper use.

poureth out--utters abundantly

(Pr 12:23),

and so disgusts others.

A wholesome tongue--(Compare Margin), pacifying and soothing
language.

tree of life--

(Pr 3:18; 11:30).

perverseness therein--cross, ill-natured language.

breach . . . spirit--(compare

Isa 65:14,

Hebrew), grieves, instead of appeasing.

primaryText.PRO:15:5: A fool despises his father’s correction, but he who heeds reproof shows prudence.
primaryText.PRO:15:6: In the house of the righteous is much treasure, but the income of the wicked brings trouble.
primaryText.PRO:15:7: The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so with the heart of fools.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 4:1; 10:17; 13:1-18).

is prudent--acts discreetly.

treasure--implying utility.

trouble--vexation and affliction.

(Compare

Pr 10:20, 21).

heart . . . not so--not right, or vain.

primaryText.PRO:15:10: There is stern discipline for one who forsakes the way. Whoever hates reproof shall die.
primaryText.PRO:15:11: Sheol and Abaddon are before the LORD— how much more then the hearts of the children of men!
primaryText.PRO:15:12: A scoffer doesn’t love to be reproved; he will not go to the wise.
primaryText.PRO:15:8: The sacrifice made by the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is his delight.
primaryText.PRO:15:9: The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who follows after righteousness.

evidence.quote:
The sacrifice [and] prayer--are acts of worship.

way . . . followeth . . . righteousness--denote conduct. God's regard
for the worship and deeds of the righteous and wicked respectively, so
stated in

Ps 50:17;
Isa 1:11.

(Compare

Pr 10:17).

the way--that in which God would have him to go

(Pr 2:13;
Ps 119:1).

Hell--

(Ps 16:10).

destruction--or, "Abaddon," the place of the destroyer. All the unseen
world is open to God, much more men's hearts.

(Compare

Pr 9:8).

go unto the wise--to be instructed.

primaryText.PRO:15:13: A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but an aching heart breaks the spirit.
primaryText.PRO:15:14: The heart of one who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly.
primaryText.PRO:15:15: All the days of the afflicted are wretched, but one who has a cheerful heart enjoys a continual feast.
primaryText.PRO:15:16: Better is little, with the fear of the LORD, than great treasure with trouble.
primaryText.PRO:15:17: Better is a dinner of herbs, where love is, than a fattened calf with hatred.

evidence.quote:
maketh . . . countenance--or, "benefits the countenance."

spirit is broken--and so the countenance is sad.

(Compare

Pr 10:21, 22).

The wise grow wiser, the fools more foolish

(Pr 9:9).

The state of the heart governs the outward condition.

evil--sad, contrasted with the cheerfulness of a feast.

trouble--agitation, implying the anxieties and perplexities
attending wealth held by worldlings

(Pr 16:18;
1Ti 6:6).

dinner--or, "allowance"

(2Ki 25:30)

--

of herbs--and that the plainest.

and hatred--(compare

Pr 10:12, 18).

primaryText.PRO:15:18: A wrathful man stirs up contention, but one who is slow to anger appeases strife.
primaryText.PRO:15:19: The way of the sluggard is like a thorn patch, but the path of the upright is a highway.
primaryText.PRO:15:20: A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish man despises his mother.
primaryText.PRO:15:21: Folly is joy to one who is void of wisdom, but a man of understanding keeps his way straight.
primaryText.PRO:15:22: Where there is no counsel, plans fail; but in a multitude of counselors they are established.
primaryText.PRO:15:23: Joy comes to a man with the reply of his mouth. How good is a word at the right time!

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 10:1).

walketh uprightly--and so finds his joy

(Pr 3:6; 10:23).

Without counsel--or, "deliberation," implying a wise deference to
the opinions of the wise and good, contrasted with rashness.
Good advice blesses the giver and receiver.

primaryText.PRO:15:24: The path of life leads upward for the wise, to keep him from going downward to Sheol.
primaryText.PRO:15:25: The LORD will uproot the house of the proud, but he will keep the widow’s borders intact.
primaryText.PRO:15:26: The LORD detests the thoughts of the wicked, but the thoughts of the pure are pleasing.
primaryText.PRO:15:27: He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house, but he who hates bribes will live.
primaryText.PRO:15:28: The heart of the righteous weighs answers, but the mouth of the wicked gushes out evil.
primaryText.PRO:15:29: The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Col 3:2).

Holy purposes prevent sinning, and so its evils.

The most desolate who have God's aid have more permanent good than
the self-reliant sinner

(Pr 2:22; 12:7).

border--or, "boundary for possessions"

(Ps 78:54).

are pleasant words--that is, pleasing to God

(Pr 8:8, 9).

(Compare

Pr 11:17).

Avarice brings trouble to him and his.

hateth gifts--or, "bribes"

(Ex 23:8;
Ps 15:5),

and is not avaricious.

(Compare

Pr 15:14; 10:11).

Caution is the fruit of wisdom; rashness of folly.

far . . . wicked--in His love and favor

(Ps 22:11; 119:155).

primaryText.PRO:15:30: The light of the eyes rejoices the heart. Good news gives health to the bones.
primaryText.PRO:15:31: The ear that listens to reproof lives, and will be at home among the wise.
primaryText.PRO:15:32: He who refuses correction despises his own soul, but he who listens to reproof gets understanding.
primaryText.PRO:15:33: The fear of the LORD teaches wisdom. Before honor is humility.

evidence.quote:
light of the eyes--

(Pr 13:9).

What gives light rejoiceth the heart, by relieving from anxiety as to
our course; so

good report--or, "doctrine"

(Isa 28:9; 53:1),

maketh . . . fat--or, "gives prosperity"

(Pr 3:13-17; 9:11).

The last clause is illustrated by the first.

(Compare

Pr 10:17).

reproof of life--which leads to life.

abideth . . . wise--is numbered among them.

refuseth--or, "neglects," "passes by"

(Pr 1:25; 4:15).

despiseth . . . soul--so acts as if esteeming its interests of no
value.

primaryText.PRO:16:1: The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD.
primaryText.PRO:16:2: All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the motives.
primaryText.PRO:16:3: Commit your deeds to the LORD, and your plans shall succeed.

evidence.quote:
preparations--schemes.

in man--or literally, "to man," belonging, or pertaining to him.

the answer . . . Lord--The efficient ordering is from God: "Man
proposes; God disposes."

clean--or, "faultless."

weigheth--or, "tries," "judges," implying that they are faulty

(Pr 21:2; 24:12).

(Compare Margin). Rely on God for success to your lawful
purposes.

primaryText.PRO:16:4: The LORD has made everything for its own end— yes, even the wicked for the day of evil.
primaryText.PRO:16:5: Everyone who is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD; they shall certainly not be unpunished.
primaryText.PRO:16:6: By mercy and truth iniquity is atoned for. By the fear of the LORD men depart from evil.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 3:32).

By mercy and truth--that is, God's

(Ps 85:10);

He effects the atonement, or covering of sin; and the principles of
true piety incline men to depart from evil; or, "mercy" and "truth" may
be man's, indicative of the gracious tempers which work instrumentally
in procuring pardon.

purged--expiated (as in

Le 16:33;
Isa 27:9,

Hebrew).

primaryText.PRO:16:7: When a man’s ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.
primaryText.PRO:16:8: Better is a little with righteousness, than great revenues with injustice.
primaryText.PRO:16:9: A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD directs his steps.

evidence.quote: Persecutions, of course, excepted.

(Compare

Pr 15:6, 16, 17).

(Compare

Pr 16:3).

directeth--establisheth.

primaryText.PRO:16:10: Inspired judgments are on the lips of the king. He shall not betray his mouth.
primaryText.PRO:16:11: Honest balances and scales are the LORD’s; all the weights in the bag are his work.
primaryText.PRO:16:12: It is an abomination for kings to do wrong, for the throne is established by righteousness.
primaryText.PRO:16:13: Righteous lips are the delight of kings. They value one who speaks the truth.
primaryText.PRO:16:14: The king’s wrath is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it.
primaryText.PRO:16:15: In the light of the king’s face is life. His favor is like a cloud of the spring rain.

evidence.quote:
The last clause depends on the first, expressing the importance
of equity in decisions, so authoritative.

are the Lord's . . . his work--that is, what He has ordered, and
hence should be observed by men.

Rulers are rightly expected, by their position, to hate evil; for
their power is sustained by righteousness.

A specification of the general sentiment of

Pr 16:12.

This wrath, so terrible and certain, like
messengers of death

(1Ki 2:25),

can be appeased by the wise.

light of . . . countenance--favor

(Ps 4:6).

life--preserves it, or gives blessings which make it valuable.

the latter rain--fell just before harvest and matured the crop; hence
specially valuable

(De 11:14).

primaryText.PRO:16:16: How much better it is to get wisdom than gold! Yes, to get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver.
primaryText.PRO:16:17: The highway of the upright is to depart from evil. He who keeps his way preserves his soul.
primaryText.PRO:16:18: Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.
primaryText.PRO:16:19: It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor, than to divide the plunder with the proud.
primaryText.PRO:16:20: He who heeds the Word finds prosperity. Whoever trusts in the LORD is blessed.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 3:16; 4:5).

The highway--A common, plain road represents the habitual
course of the righteous in departing from evil.

keepeth--observes.

(Compare

Pr 15:33).

Haughtiness and pride imply self-confidence which produces
carelessness, and hence

a fall--literally, "sliding."

divide the spoil--that is, conquer. Avoid the society of the proud

(Jas 4:6).

handleth a matter--wisely considers "the word," that is, of God
(compare

Pr 13:13).

trusteth--(Compare

Ps 2:12; 118:8, 9).

primaryText.PRO:16:21: The wise in heart shall be called prudent. Pleasantness of the lips promotes instruction.
primaryText.PRO:16:22: Understanding is a fountain of life to one who has it, but the punishment of fools is their folly.
primaryText.PRO:16:23: The heart of the wise instructs his mouth, and adds learning to his lips.
primaryText.PRO:16:24: Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
primaryText.PRO:16:25: There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death.

evidence.quote:
wise in heart--who rightly consider duty.

sweetness of the lips--eloquent discourse, persuades and instructs
others.

Understanding--or, "discretion," is a constant source of blessing

(Pr 13:14),

benefiting others; but fools' best efforts are folly.
The heart is the source of wisdom flowing from the mouth.

(Compare

Pr 15:26).

Gentle, kind words, by soothing the mind, give the body health.

(Compare

Pr 14:2).

primaryText.PRO:16:26: The appetite of the laboring man labors for him, for his mouth urges him on.
primaryText.PRO:16:27: A worthless man devises mischief. His speech is like a scorching fire.
primaryText.PRO:16:28: A perverse man stirs up strife. A whisperer separates close friends.
primaryText.PRO:16:29: A man of violence entices his neighbor, and leads him in a way that is not good.
primaryText.PRO:16:30: One who winks his eyes to plot perversities, one who compresses his lips, is bent on evil.

evidence.quote: Diligence is a duty due to one's self, for his wants require labor.

ungodly man--(Compare

Pr 6:12).

diggeth up evil--labors for it.

in his lips . . . fire--His words are calumniating

(Jas 3:6).

(Compare

Pr 6:14; 10:31).

whisperer--prater, talebearer

(Pr 18:8; 26:20).

violent man--or, "man of mischief"

(Pr 3:31).

enticeth--

(Pr 1:10).

He shutteth his eyes--denoting deep thought

(Ps 64:6).

moving his lips--or, "biting his lips"--a determined purpose

(Pr 6:13).

primaryText.PRO:16:31: Gray hair is a crown of glory. It is attained by a life of righteousness.
primaryText.PRO:16:32: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty; one who rules his spirit, than he who takes a city.
primaryText.PRO:16:33: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 20:29).

if--or, which may be supplied properly, or without it the
sense is as in

Pr 3:16; 4:10,

that piety is blessed with long life.

(Compare

Pr 14:29).

taketh a city--that is, by fighting.
Seemingly the most fortuitous events are ordered by God.

primaryText.PRO:17:1: Better is a dry morsel with quietness, than a house full of feasting with strife.
primaryText.PRO:17:2: A servant who deals wisely will rule over a son who causes shame, and shall have a part in the inheritance among the brothers.
primaryText.PRO:17:3: The refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, but the LORD tests the hearts.

evidence.quote:
sacrifices--or, "feasts" made with part of them (compare

Pr 7:14;
Le 2:3; 7:31).

with--literally, "of."

strife--its product, or attendant.

(Compare

Pr 14:35).

causeth shame--

(Pr 10:5).

shall . . . inheritance--that is, share a brother's part (compare

Nu 27:4, 7).

God only knows, as He tries

(Ps 12:6; 66:10)

the heart.

primaryText.PRO:17:4: An evildoer heeds wicked lips. A liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue.
primaryText.PRO:17:5: Whoever mocks the poor reproaches his Maker. He who is glad at calamity shall not be unpunished.
