primaryText.PRO:17:6: Children’s children are the crown of old men; the glory of children is their parents.

evidence.quote: Wicked doers and speakers alike delight in calumny.

(Compare

Pr 14:31).

glad at calamities--rejoicing in others' evil. Such are rightly
punished by God, who knows their hearts.

Prolonged posterity is a blessing, its cutting off a curse

(Pr 13:22;
Ps 109:13-15),

hence children may glory in virtuous ancestry.

primaryText.PRO:17:7: Excellent speech isn’t fitting for a fool, much less do lying lips fit a prince.
primaryText.PRO:17:8: A bribe is a precious stone in the eyes of him who gives it; wherever he turns, he prospers.
primaryText.PRO:17:9: He who covers an offense promotes love; but he who repeats a matter separates best friends.

evidence.quote:
Excellent speech--(Compare Margin). Such language as ill suits
a fool, as lying (ought to suit) a prince

(Pr 16:12, 13).

One so corrupt as to take a bribe evinces his high estimate of it
by subjection to its influence

(Pr 18:16; 19:6).

seeketh love--(Compare Margin). The contrast is between the
peace-maker and tale-bearer.

primaryText.PRO:17:10: A rebuke enters deeper into one who has understanding than a hundred lashes into a fool.
primaryText.PRO:17:11: An evil man seeks only rebellion; therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him.
primaryText.PRO:17:12: Let a bear robbed of her cubs meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly.

evidence.quote: Reproof more affects the wise than severe scourging, fools.

Such meet just retribution

(1Ki 2:25).

a cruel messenger--one to inflict it.
They are less rational in anger than wild beasts.

primaryText.PRO:17:13: Whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house.
primaryText.PRO:17:14: The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam, therefore stop contention before quarreling breaks out.
primaryText.PRO:17:15: He who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the righteous, both of them alike are an abomination to the LORD.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Ps 7:4; 35:12).

evil--injury to another

(Pr 13:21).

letteth . . . water--as a breach in a dam.

before . . . meddled with--before strife has become sharp, or, by an
explanation better suiting the figure, before it rolls on, or
increases.

abomination . . . Lord--as reversing His method of acting

(Pr 3:32; 12:2).

primaryText.PRO:17:16: Why is there money in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, since he has no understanding?
primaryText.PRO:17:17: A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity.
primaryText.PRO:17:18: A man void of understanding strikes hands, and becomes collateral in the presence of his neighbor.

evidence.quote:
Though wealth cannot buy wisdom for those who do not love it, yet
wisdom procures wealth

(Pr 3:16; 14:24).

To the second of these parallel clauses, there is an accession of
meaning, that is, that a brother's love is specially seen in adversity.

(Compare

Pr 6:1-5; 11:15).

in the presence, &c.--that is, he either fails to consult his friend,
or to follow his advice.

primaryText.PRO:17:19: He who loves disobedience loves strife. One who builds a high gate seeks destruction.
primaryText.PRO:17:20: One who has a perverse heart doesn’t find prosperity, and one who has a deceitful tongue falls into trouble.
primaryText.PRO:17:21: He who becomes the father of a fool grieves. The father of a fool has no joy.
primaryText.PRO:17:22: A cheerful heart makes good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.

evidence.quote:
strife--contention is, and leads to, sin.

he that exalteth his gate--gratifies a vain love of costly building.

seeketh--or, "findeth," as if he sought (compare "loveth death,"

Pr 8:36).

The second clause advances on the first. The ill-natured fail of
good, and the cavilling and fault-finding incur evil.

(Compare

Pr 23:24).

Different words are rendered by "fool," both denoting stupidity and
impiety.

(Compare

Pr 14:30; 15:13).

The effect of the mind on the body is well known.

medicine--or, "body," which better corresponds with "bone."

drieth--as if the marrow were exhausted.

primaryText.PRO:17:23: A wicked man receives a bribe in secret, to pervert the ways of justice.
primaryText.PRO:17:24: Wisdom is before the face of one who has understanding, but the eyes of a fool wander to the ends of the earth.
primaryText.PRO:17:25: A foolish son brings grief to his father, and bitterness to her who bore him.
primaryText.PRO:17:26: Also to punish the righteous is not good, nor to flog officials for their integrity.

evidence.quote:
a gift . . . bosom--Money and other valuables were borne in a fold
of the garment, called the bosom.

to pervert--that is, by bribery.

Wisdom . . . him--ever an object of regard, while a fool's
affections are unsettled.

a grief--or cross, vexation (compare

Pr 17:21; 10:1).

Also--that is, Equally to be avoided are other sins: punishing good
subjects, or resisting good rulers.

primaryText.PRO:17:27: He who spares his words has knowledge. He who is even tempered is a man of understanding.
primaryText.PRO:17:28: Even a fool, when he keeps silent, is counted wise. When he shuts his lips, he is thought to be discerning.

evidence.quote:
Prudence of speech is commended as is an excellent or calm
spirit, not excited to vain conversation.

primaryText.PRO:18:1: A man who isolates himself pursues selfishness, and defies all sound judgment.
primaryText.PRO:18:2: A fool has no delight in understanding, but only in revealing his own opinion.
primaryText.PRO:18:3: When wickedness comes, contempt also comes, and with shame comes disgrace.

evidence.quote:
Through desire . . . seeketh--that is, seeks selfish gratification.

intermeddleth . . . wisdom--or, "rushes on"

(Pr 17:14)

against all wisdom, or what is valuable

(Pr 2:7).

that his heart . . . itself--that is, takes pleasure in revealing
his folly

(Pr 12:23; 15:2).

So surely are sin and punishment connected

(Pr 16:4).

wicked, for "wickedness," answers to

ignominy, or the state of such; and

contempt, the feeling of others to them; and to

reproach, a manifestation of contempt.

primaryText.PRO:18:4: The words of a man’s mouth are like deep waters. The fountain of wisdom is like a flowing brook.
primaryText.PRO:18:5: To be partial to the faces of the wicked is not good, nor to deprive the innocent of justice.

evidence.quote: Wise speech is like an exhaustless stream of benefit.

accept the person--(Compare

Ps 82:2).

"It is not good" is to be supplied before "to overthrow."

primaryText.PRO:18:6: A fool’s lips come into strife, and his mouth invites beatings.
primaryText.PRO:18:7: A fool’s mouth is his destruction, and his lips are a snare to his soul.
primaryText.PRO:18:8: The words of a gossip are like dainty morsels: they go down into a person’s innermost parts.

evidence.quote:
The quarrelsome bring trouble on themselves. Their rash language
ensnares them

(Pr 6:2).

(Compare

Pr 16:28).

as wounds--not sustained by the Hebrew; better, as "sweet morsels,"
which men gladly swallow.

innermost . . . belly--the mind, or heart (compare

Pr 20:27-30;
Ps 22:14).

primaryText.PRO:18:10: The LORD’s name is a strong tower: the righteous run to him, and are safe.
primaryText.PRO:18:11: The rich man’s wealth is his strong city, like an unscalable wall in his own imagination.
primaryText.PRO:18:9: One who is slack in his work is brother to him who is a master of destruction.

evidence.quote:
One by failing to get, the other by wasting wealth, grows poor.

waster--literally, "master of washing," a prodigal.

name of the Lord--manifested perfections

(Ps 8:1; 20:2),

as faithfulness, power, mercy, &c., on which men rely.

is safe--literally, "set on high, out of danger"

(Ps 18:2; 91:4).

contrasts with

Pr 18:10

(compare

Pr 10:15).

Such is a vain trust (compare

Ps 73:6).

primaryText.PRO:18:12: Before destruction the heart of man is proud, but before honor is humility.
primaryText.PRO:18:13: He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.
primaryText.PRO:18:14: A man’s spirit will sustain him in sickness, but a crushed spirit, who can bear?

evidence.quote:
Hasty speech evinces self-conceit, and ensures shame

(Pr 26:12).

infirmity--bodily sickness, or outward evil. The spirit, which sustains, being wounded, no support is left, except, as implied,
in God.

primaryText.PRO:18:15: The heart of the discerning gets knowledge. The ear of the wise seeks knowledge.
primaryText.PRO:18:16: A man’s gift makes room for him, and brings him before great men.
primaryText.PRO:18:17: He who pleads his cause first seems right— until another comes and questions him.
primaryText.PRO:18:18: The lot settles disputes, and keeps strong ones apart.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 1:5, 15, 31).

(Compare

Pr 17:8, 23).

Disapproval of the fact stated is implied.

One-sided statements are not reliable.

searcheth--thoroughly

(Pr 17:9, 19).

The lot--whose disposal is of God

(Pr 16:13),

may, properly used, be a right mode of settling disputes.

primaryText.PRO:18:19: A brother offended is more difficult than a fortified city. Disputes are like the bars of a fortress.
primaryText.PRO:18:20: A man’s stomach is filled with the fruit of his mouth. With the harvest of his lips he is satisfied.
primaryText.PRO:18:21: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

evidence.quote:
No feuds so difficult of adjustment as those of relatives; hence
great care should be used to avoid them.

(Compare

Pr 12:14; 13:2).

Men's words are the fruit, or, increase of his lips, and
when good, benefit them.

satisfied with--(Compare

Pr 1:31; 14:14).

Death and life--or, the greatest evil and good.

that love it--that is, the tongue, or its use for good or evil.

eat . . . fruit--(Compare

Pr 18:19;
Jas 1:19).

primaryText.PRO:18:22: Whoever finds a wife finds a good thing, and obtains favor of the LORD.
primaryText.PRO:18:23: The poor plead for mercy, but the rich answer harshly.
primaryText.PRO:18:24: A man of many companions may be ruined, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.

evidence.quote:
The old versions supply "good" before the "wife," as the last
clause and

Pr 19:14

imply (compare

Pr 31:10).

the rich . . . roughly--He is tolerated because rich, implying that
the estimate of men by wealth is wrong.

A man . . . friendly--better, "A man . . . (is) to, or, may
triumph

(Ps 108:9),

or, shout for joy

(Ps 5:11),

that is, may congratulate himself." Indeed, there is a Friend who is
better than a brother; such is the "Friend of sinners"

[Mt 11:19;
Lu 7:34],

who may have been before the writer's mind.

primaryText.PRO:19:1: Better is the poor who walks in his integrity than he who is perverse in his lips and is a fool.
primaryText.PRO:19:2: It isn’t good to have zeal without knowledge, nor to be hasty with one’s feet and miss the way.
primaryText.PRO:19:3: The foolishness of man subverts his way; his heart rages against the LORD.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 28:6).

"Rich" for fool here. Integrity is better than riches

(Pr 15:16, 17; 16:8).

The last illustrates the first clause. Rashness, the result of
ignorance, brings trouble.

primaryText.PRO:19:4: Wealth adds many friends, but the poor is separated from his friend.
primaryText.PRO:19:5: A false witness shall not be unpunished. He who pours out lies shall not go free.
primaryText.PRO:19:6: Many will entreat the favor of a ruler, and everyone is a friend to a man who gives gifts.
primaryText.PRO:19:7: All the relatives of the poor shun him; how much more do his friends avoid him! He pursues them with pleas, but they are gone.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 14:20).

Such facts are often adduced with implied disapprobation.

Pr 19:9,

where perish explains not escape here (compare

Ps 88:9, 10).

primaryText.PRO:19:10: Delicate living is not appropriate for a fool, much less for a servant to have rule over princes.
primaryText.PRO:19:11: The discretion of a man makes him slow to anger. It is his glory to overlook an offense.
primaryText.PRO:19:8: He who gets wisdom loves his own soul. He who keeps understanding shall find good.
primaryText.PRO:19:9: A false witness shall not be unpunished. He who utters lies shall perish.

evidence.quote:
(Compare Margin;

Pr 15:32).

loveth . . . soul--or, "himself," which he evinces by regarding his
best interests.

keepeth--or, "regards."

(Compare

Pr 17:7).

The fool is incapable of properly using pleasure as knowledge, yet for
him to have it is less incongruous than the undue elevation of
servants. Let each abide in his calling

(1Co 7:20).

(Compare

Pr 14:29; 16:32).

This inculcation of a forgiving spirit shows that true religion is
always the same

(Mt 5:22-24).

primaryText.PRO:19:12: The king’s wrath is like the roaring of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass.
primaryText.PRO:19:13: A foolish son is the calamity of his father. A wife’s quarrels are a continual dripping.
primaryText.PRO:19:14: House and riches are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 16:14, 15; 20:2).

A motive to submission to lawful authority.

calamity--literally, "calamities," varied and many.

continual dropping--a perpetual annoyance, wearing out patience.

A contrast of men's gifts and God's, who, though author of both
blessings, confers the latter by His more special providence.

and--or, "but," implying that the evils of

Pr 19:13

are only avoided by His care.

primaryText.PRO:19:15: Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep. The idle soul shall suffer hunger.
primaryText.PRO:19:16: He who keeps the commandment keeps his soul, but he who is contemptuous in his ways shall die.
primaryText.PRO:19:17: He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD; he will reward him.
primaryText.PRO:19:18: Discipline your son, for there is hope; don’t be a willing party to his death.

evidence.quote:
a deep sleep--a state of utter indifference.

idle soul--or, "person" (compare

Pr 10:4; 12:24).

(Compare

Pr 10:17; 13:13).

despiseth . . . ways--opposed to keeping or observing, neglects

(Pr 16:17)

(as unworthy of regard) his moral conduct.

(Compare

Pr 14:21;
Ps 37:26).

hath pity--shown by acts (compare Margin).

(Compare

Pr 13:24; 23:13).

let not . . . spare--literally, "do not lift up thy soul"

(Ps 24:4; 25:1),

that is, do not desire to his death; a caution to passionate parents
against angry chastisement.

primaryText.PRO:19:19: A hot-tempered man must pay the penalty, for if you rescue him, you must do it again.
primaryText.PRO:19:20: Listen to counsel and receive instruction, that you may be wise in your latter end.
primaryText.PRO:19:21: There are many plans in a man’s heart, but the LORD’s counsel will prevail.

evidence.quote: Repeated efforts of kindness are lost on ill-natured persons.

(Compare

Pr 13:18-20).

latter end--

(Pr 5:11).

In youth prepare for age.

(Compare

Pr 16:1, 9;
Ps 33:10, 11).

The failure of man's devices is implied.

primaryText.PRO:19:22: That which makes a man to be desired is his kindness. A poor man is better than a liar.
primaryText.PRO:19:23: The fear of the LORD leads to life, then contentment; he rests and will not be touched by trouble.
primaryText.PRO:19:24: The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; he will not so much as bring it to his mouth again.

evidence.quote:
desire--that is, to do good, indicates a kind disposition

(Pr 11:23);

and the poor thus affected are better than liars, who say and do
not.

The fear . . . life--(Compare

Pr 3:2).

abide--or, "remain contented"

(1Ti 4:8).

not visited with evil--

(Pr 10:3;
Ps 37:25),

as a judgment, in which sense visit is often used

(Ps 89:32;
Jer 6:15).

bosom--literally, a wide dish in which the hand was plunged in
eating

(Mt 26:23).

Compare

Pr 26:15,

the sentiment expressed with equal irony and less exaggeration.

primaryText.PRO:19:25: Flog a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; rebuke one who has understanding, and he will gain knowledge.
primaryText.PRO:19:26: He who robs his father and drives away his mother is a son who causes shame and brings reproach.
primaryText.PRO:19:27: If you stop listening to instruction, my son, you will stray from the words of knowledge.

evidence.quote:
Such is the benefit of reproof; even the simple profit, much more
the wise.
Avoid whatever leads from truth.

primaryText.PRO:19:28: A corrupt witness mocks justice, and the mouth of the wicked gulps down iniquity.
primaryText.PRO:19:29: Penalties are prepared for scoffers, and beatings for the backs of fools.

evidence.quote:
ungodly witness--(Compare Margin), one false by bad principles
(compare

Pr 6:12).

scorneth judgment--sets at naught the dictates of justice.

devoureth--literally, "swalloweth," as something delightful.

Their punishment is sure, fixed, and ready (compare

Pr 3:34; 10:13).

primaryText.PRO:20:1: Wine is a mocker and beer is a brawler. Whoever is led astray by them is not wise.
primaryText.PRO:20:2: The terror of a king is like the roaring of a lion. He who provokes him to anger forfeits his own life.
primaryText.PRO:20:3: It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling.

evidence.quote:
mocker--scorner. Such men are made by wine.

strong drink--made by spicing wine (compare

Isa 5:11, 22);

and it may include wine.

raging--or boisterous as a drunkard.

deceived--literally, "erring," or reeling.

(Compare

Pr 19:12).

Men who resist authority injure themselves

(Ro 13:2).

to cease from strife--or, better, "to dwell from or without strife,"
denoting the habit of life.

fool . . . meddling--

(Pr 17:14).

primaryText.PRO:20:4: The sluggard will not plow by reason of the winter; therefore he shall beg in harvest, and have nothing.
primaryText.PRO:20:5: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.
primaryText.PRO:20:6: Many men claim to be men of unfailing love, but who can find a faithful man?
primaryText.PRO:20:7: A righteous man walks in integrity. Blessed are his children after him.

evidence.quote:
shall . . . beg--literally, "ask" (in this sense,

Ps 109:10).

Counsel . . . water--that is, deeply hidden

(Pr 18:4;
Ps 13:2).

The wise can discern well.

Boasters are unreliable.

goodness--or, "kind disposition."

The conduct of good men proclaims their sound principles. God's
covenant and their good example secure blessing to their children

(Pr 4:26;
Ps 112:1, 2).

primaryText.PRO:20:10: Differing weights and differing measures, both of them alike are an abomination to the LORD.
primaryText.PRO:20:11: Even a child makes himself known by his doings, whether his work is pure, and whether it is right.
primaryText.PRO:20:12: The hearing ear, and the seeing eye, the LORD has made even both of them.
primaryText.PRO:20:8: A king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters away all evil with his eyes.
primaryText.PRO:20:9: Who can say, “I have made my heart pure. I am clean and without sin”?

evidence.quote:
As in

Pr 14:35; 16:10, 15,

this is the character of a good king, not of all kings.

The interrogation in the affirmative strengthens the implied
negation (compare

Job 15:14;
Ec 7:20).

Various measures, implying that some are wrong (compare

Pr 11:1; 16:11).

The conduct of children even is the best test of principle (compare

Mt 7:16).

Hence, of course, God will know all you do

(Ps 94:9).

primaryText.PRO:20:13: Don’t love sleep, lest you come to poverty. Open your eyes, and you shall be satisfied with bread.
primaryText.PRO:20:14: “It’s no good, it’s no good,” says the buyer; but when he is gone his way, then he boasts.
primaryText.PRO:20:15: There is gold and abundance of rubies, but the lips of knowledge are a rare jewel.
primaryText.PRO:20:16: Take the garment of one who puts up collateral for a stranger; and hold him in pledge for a wayward woman.

evidence.quote:
Activity and diligence contrasted with sloth

(Pr 6:9; 10:11).

lest . . . poverty--literally, "be deprived of inheritance."

when . . . his way--implying that he goes about boasting of his
bargains.

The contrast denotes the greater value of knowledge (compare

Pr 3:14-16).

Take his garment--implies severe exaction, justified by the
surety's rashness.

a strange woman--by some readings "strangers," but the former here,
and in

Pr 27:13,

is allowable, and strengthens the sense. The debauchee is less reliable
than the merely careless.

primaryText.PRO:20:17: Fraudulent food is sweet to a man, but afterwards his mouth is filled with gravel.
primaryText.PRO:20:18: Plans are established by advice; by wise guidance you wage war!
primaryText.PRO:20:19: He who goes about as a tale-bearer reveals secrets; therefore don’t keep company with him who opens wide his lips.
primaryText.PRO:20:20: Whoever curses his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in blackness of darkness.

evidence.quote:
Bread . . . sweet--either as unlawfully

(Pr 9:17)

or easily obtained.

mouth . . . gravel--well expresses the pain and grief given
at last.

(Compare

Pr 15:22).

Be careful and considerate in important plans.

Those who love to tell news will hardly keep secrets.

flattereth . . . lips--(compare Margin;

Pr 1:10).

meddle . . . him--literally, "join," or "associate with."

his lamp--(Compare

Pr 13:9; 24:20).

primaryText.PRO:20:21: An inheritance quickly gained at the beginning won’t be blessed in the end.
primaryText.PRO:20:22: Don’t say, “I will pay back evil.” Wait for the LORD, and he will save you.
primaryText.PRO:20:23: The LORD detests differing weights, and dishonest scales are not pleasing.
primaryText.PRO:20:24: A man’s steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way?

evidence.quote:
gotten hastily--contrary to God's providence

(Pr 28:20),

implying its unjust or easy attainment; hence the man is punished, or
spends freely what he got easily (compare

Pr 20:17).

(Compare

Pr 20:10; 11:1).

Man's goings--literally, "Stately steppings of a strong man."

a man--any common man.

understand--or, "perceive."

primaryText.PRO:20:25: It is a snare to a man to make a rash dedication, then later to consider his vows.

evidence.quote:
devoureth . . . holy--or, better, "who rashly speaks promises,"
or "devotes what is holy," consecrating any thing. This suits better the
last clause, which expresses a similar view of the results of rashly
vowing.

primaryText.PRO:20:26: A wise king winnows out the wicked, and drives the threshing wheel over them.
primaryText.PRO:20:27: The spirit of man is the LORD’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.
primaryText.PRO:20:28: Love and faithfulness keep the king safe. His throne is sustained by love.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 20:8).

bringeth . . . over them--The wheel was used for threshing grain. The
figure denotes severity (compare

Am 1:3).

primaryText.PRO:20:29: The glory of young men is their strength. The splendor of old men is their gray hair.
primaryText.PRO:20:30: Wounding blows cleanse away evil, and beatings purge the innermost parts.

evidence.quote:
The glory of young men . . . the beauty of old men--Each
age has its peculiar excellence

(Pr 16:31).

blueness--literally, "joining," the process of uniting the edges
of a wound throws off purulent matter.

stripes . . . belly--So punishment provides healing of soul

(Pr 18:8),

by deterring from evil courses.

primaryText.PRO:21:1: The king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand like the watercourses. He turns it wherever he desires.
primaryText.PRO:21:2: Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the hearts.
primaryText.PRO:21:3: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.
primaryText.PRO:21:4: A high look and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, is sin.

evidence.quote:
rivers--irrigating channels

(Ps 1:3),

whose course was easily turned (compare

De 11:10).

God disposes even kings as He pleases

(Pr 16:9;
Ps 33:15).

high look--(Compare Margin;

Ps 131:1).

proud heart--or, "heart of breadth," one that is swollen (compare

Ps 101:5).

ploughing--better "lamp," a frequent figure for prosperity

(Pr 20:20);

hence joy or delight.

primaryText.PRO:21:5: The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit; and everyone who is hasty surely rushes to poverty.
primaryText.PRO:21:6: Getting treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor for those who seek death.
primaryText.PRO:21:7: The violence of the wicked will drive them away, because they refuse to do what is right.
primaryText.PRO:21:8: The way of the guilty is devious, but the conduct of the innocent is upright.

evidence.quote:
The contrast is between steady industry and rashness (compare

Pr 19:2).

The getting--or, "what is obtained" (compare

Job 7:2;
Jer 22:13,

Hebrew).

vanity . . . to and fro--as fleeting as chaff or stubble in the wind
(compare

Pr 20:17-21;
Ps 62:10).

them . . . death--act as if they did

(Pr 8:36; 17:19).

robbery--or, "destruction," especially oppression, of which they
are authors.

shall destroy--literally, "cut with a saw"

(1Ki 7:9),

that is, utterly ruin them. Their sins shall be visited on them in

to do judgment--what is just and right.

of man--any one; his way is opposed to truth, and also estranged

primaryText.PRO:21:10: The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.
primaryText.PRO:21:11: When the mocker is punished, the simple gains wisdom. When the wise is instructed, he receives knowledge.
primaryText.PRO:21:12: The Righteous One considers the house of the wicked, and brings the wicked to ruin.
primaryText.PRO:21:13: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
primaryText.PRO:21:9: It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop than to share a house with a contentious woman.

evidence.quote:
corner--a turret or arbor on the roof.

brawling--or contentious.

wide house--literally, "house of fellowship," large enough for several
families.

So strongly does he desire to do evil

(Ps 10:3;
Ec 8:11),

that he will not even spare his friend if in his way.

(Compare

Pr 19:25).

That which the simple learn by the terrors of punishment, the wise
learn by teaching.

(Compare

Ps 37:35-38; 73:17, 20).

house--family or interests.

overthroweth--either supply "God" (compare

Pr 10:24),

or the word is used impersonally.

primaryText.PRO:21:14: A gift in secret pacifies anger, and a bribe in the cloak, strong wrath.
primaryText.PRO:21:15: It is joy to the righteous to do justice; but it is a destruction to the workers of iniquity.
primaryText.PRO:21:16: The man who wanders out of the way of understanding shall rest in the assembly of the departed spirits.
primaryText.PRO:21:17: He who loves pleasure will be a poor man. He who loves wine and oil won’t be rich.
primaryText.PRO:21:18: The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, the treacherous for the upright.

evidence.quote:
The effect of bribery

(Pr 17:23)

is enhanced by secrecy, as the bribed person does not wish his motives
made known.

But the just love right and need no bribes. The wicked at last meet
destruction, though for a time happy in concealing corruption.

the way of understanding--(Compare

Pr 12:26; 14:22).

remain--that is, rest as at a journey's end; death will be his
unchanging home.
Costly luxuries impoverish.

(Compare

Pr 11:8).

By suffering what they had devised for the righteous, or brought on
them, the wicked became their ransom, in the usual sense of substitutes
(compare

Jos 7:26;
Es 7:9).

primaryText.PRO:21:19: It is better to dwell in a desert land, than with a contentious and fretful woman.
primaryText.PRO:21:20: There is precious treasure and oil in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man swallows it up.
primaryText.PRO:21:21: He who follows after righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.
primaryText.PRO:21:22: A wise man scales the city of the mighty, and brings down the strength of its confidence.
primaryText.PRO:21:23: Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue keeps his soul from troubles.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 21:9).

wilderness--pasture, though uninhabitable ground

(Ps 65:12).

The wise, by diligence and care, lay up and increase wealth, while
fools

spend--literally, "swallow it up," greedily.

He who tries to act justly and kindly

(Ps 34:14)

will prosper and obtain justice and honor.

"Wisdom is better than strength"

(Ec 7:19; 9:15).

strength . . . thereof--that in which they confide.

primaryText.PRO:21:24: The proud and arrogant man—“Scoffer” is his name— he works in the arrogance of pride.
primaryText.PRO:21:25: The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor.
primaryText.PRO:21:26: There are those who covet greedily all day long; but the righteous give and don’t withhold.
primaryText.PRO:21:27: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination— how much more, when he brings it with a wicked mind!

evidence.quote:
The reproachful name is deserved by those who treat others with
anger and contempt.

desire--that is, of ease and idleness brings him to
starvation.

The sin of covetousness marks the sluggard, as the virtue of
benevolence the righteous.

God regards the heart, and hypocrisy is more odious than open
inconsistency.

wicked mind--or, "design"

(Pr 1:4).

primaryText.PRO:21:28: A false witness will perish. A man who listens speaks to eternity.

primaryText.PRO:21:30: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD.
primaryText.PRO:21:31: The horse is prepared for the day of battle; but victory is with the LORD.

evidence.quote:

that heareth--or heeds instruction, and so grows wise.

speaketh constantly--or sincerely (compare

Jas 1:19).

hardeneth his face--is obstinate.

directeth . . . way--considers it, and acts advisedly.

Men's best devices and reliances are vain compared with God's,
or without His aid

(Pr 19:21;
Ps 20:7; 33:17).

primaryText.PRO:22:1: A good name is more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold.
primaryText.PRO:22:2: The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is the maker of them all.
primaryText.PRO:22:3: A prudent man sees danger and hides himself; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it.
primaryText.PRO:22:4: The result of humility and the fear of the LORD is wealth, honor, and life.

evidence.quote:
A good name--

(Job 30:8,

Hebrew); "good" is supplied here from

Ec 7:1.

loving favour--kind regard, that is, of the wise and good.

Before God all are on the same footing

(Pr 14:31; 17:5).

are punished--that is, for their temerity; for the evil is not
necessarily punitive, as the prudent might otherwise be its objects.

humility and the fear of the Lord--are in apposition; one produces
the other. On the results, compare

Pr 3:16; 8:18.

primaryText.PRO:22:5: Thorns and snares are in the path of the wicked; whoever guards his soul stays far from them.
primaryText.PRO:22:6: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.
primaryText.PRO:22:7: The rich rule over the poor. The borrower is servant to the lender.
primaryText.PRO:22:8: He who sows wickedness reaps trouble, and the rod of his fury will be destroyed.

evidence.quote:
he that . . . them--Those who properly watch over their own souls
are thus preserved from the dangers which attend the way of perverse men

(Pr 16:17).

Train--initiate, or early instruct.

the way--literally, "his way," that selected for him in which he should
go; for early training secures habitual walking in it.

The influence of wealth sets aside moral distinctions is implied,
and, of course, disapproved (compare

Pr 19:6; 21:14,

&c.).

primaryText.PRO:22:10: Drive out the mocker, and strife will go out; yes, quarrels and insults will stop.
primaryText.PRO:22:11: He who loves purity of heart and speaks gracefully is the king’s friend.
primaryText.PRO:22:12: The LORD’s eyes watch over knowledge, but he frustrates the words of the unfaithful.
primaryText.PRO:22:9: He who has a generous eye will be blessed, for he shares his food with the poor.

evidence.quote:
a bountiful eye--that is, a beneficent disposition.

for he giveth . . . poor--His acts prove it.

Cast out--or drive away. Scorners foster strife by taunts and
revilings.

(Compare Margin).

pureness of heart--and gentle, kind words win favor, even from kings.

preserve--or guard.

knowledge--its principles and possessors.

overthroweth--utterly confounds and destroys the wicked.

primaryText.PRO:22:13: The sluggard says, “There is a lion outside! I will be killed in the streets!”
primaryText.PRO:22:14: The mouth of an adulteress is a deep pit. He who is under the LORD’s wrath will fall into it.
primaryText.PRO:22:15: Folly is bound up in the heart of a child; the rod of discipline drives it far from him.
primaryText.PRO:22:16: Whoever oppresses the poor for his own increase and whoever gives to the rich, both come to poverty.

evidence.quote: Frivolous excuses satisfy the indolent man's conscience.

The mouth--or flattering speeches

(Pr 5:3; 7:5)

ensnare man, as pits, beasts. God makes their own sin their
punishment.

is bound--or firmly fixed. Chastisement deters from crime and so
leads to reformation of principle.

These two vices pertain to the same selfish feeling. Both are
deservedly odious to God and incur punishment.

primaryText.PRO:22:17: Turn your ear, and listen to the words of the wise. Apply your heart to my teaching.
primaryText.PRO:22:18: For it is a pleasant thing if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips.
primaryText.PRO:22:19: I teach you today, even you, so that your trust may be in the LORD.
primaryText.PRO:22:20: Haven’t I written to you thirty excellent things of counsel and knowledge,
primaryText.PRO:22:21: To teach you truth, reliable words, to give sound answers to the ones who sent you?

evidence.quote:
Here begins another division of the book, marked by those
encouragements to the pursuit of wisdom, which are found in the earlier
chapters. It will be observed that at

Pr 22:22-24:12,

the proverbs are generally expressed in two verses instead of one (see

Introduction).

These lessons must be laid up in the mind, and

fitted--or better, "fixed" in the lips so as to be ever ready.
That . . . Lord--This is the design of the instruction.

excellent things--or probably of former times.

counsels and knowledge--both advice and instruction.

Specially he desires to secure accuracy, so that his pupil may
teach others.

primaryText.PRO:22:22: Don’t exploit the poor because he is poor; and don’t crush the needy in court;
primaryText.PRO:22:23: for the LORD will plead their case, and plunder the life of those who plunder them.

evidence.quote:
Here follow ten precepts of two verses each. Though men fail
to defend the poor, God will

(Pr 17:5;
Ps 12:5).

in the gate--place of public gathering

(Job 5:4;
Ps 69:12).

primaryText.PRO:22:24: Don’t befriend a hot-tempered man. Don’t associate with one who harbors anger,
primaryText.PRO:22:25: lest you learn his ways and ensnare your soul.

evidence.quote:
a snare . . . soul--The unsuspecting are often misled by bad
company.

primaryText.PRO:22:26: Don’t you be one of those who strike hands, of those who are collateral for debts.
primaryText.PRO:22:27: If you don’t have means to pay, why should he take away your bed from under you?

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 6:1; 17:18).
should he take, &c.--that is, the creditor.

primaryText.PRO:22:28: Don’t move the ancient boundary stone which your fathers have set up.
primaryText.PRO:22:29: Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings. He won’t serve obscure men.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 23:10).

Do not entrench on others

(De 19:14; 27:17).

Success rewards diligence

(Pr 10:4; 21:5).

primaryText.PRO:23:1: When you sit to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before you;
primaryText.PRO:23:2: put a knife to your throat if you are a man given to appetite.
primaryText.PRO:23:3: Don’t be desirous of his dainties, since they are deceitful food.

evidence.quote: Avoid the dangers of gluttony.

put a knife--an Eastern figure for putting restraint on the
appetite.
are deceitful meat--though well tasted, injurious.

primaryText.PRO:23:4: Don’t weary yourself to be rich. In your wisdom, show restraint.
primaryText.PRO:23:5: Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

1Ti 6:9, 10).

thine own wisdom--which regards riches intrinsically as a blessing.

Wilt . . . eyes--As the eyes fly after or seek riches, they are not,
that is, either become transitory or unsatisfying; fully expressed by
their flying away.

primaryText.PRO:23:6: Don’t eat the food of him who has a stingy eye, and don’t crave his delicacies,
primaryText.PRO:23:7: for as he thinks about the cost, so he is. “Eat and drink!” he says to you, but his heart is not with you.
primaryText.PRO:23:8: You will vomit up the morsel which you have eaten and waste your pleasant words.

evidence.quote:
The morsel . . . words--that is, disgusted with his true character,
all pleasant intercourse will be destroyed.

primaryText.PRO:23:9: Don’t speak in the ears of a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 9:8).

"Cast not your pearls before swine"

(Mt 7:6).

primaryText.PRO:23:10: Don’t move the ancient boundary stone. Don’t encroach on the fields of the fatherless,
primaryText.PRO:23:11: for their Defender is strong. He will plead their case against you.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 22:22, 23).

redeemer--or avenger

(Le 25:25, 26;
Nu 35:12),

hence advocate

(Job 19:25).

plead . . . thee--(Compare

Job 31:21;
Ps 35:1; 68:5).

primaryText.PRO:23:12: Apply your heart to instruction, and your ears to the words of knowledge.
primaryText.PRO:23:13: Don’t withhold correction from a child. If you punish him with the rod, he will not die.
primaryText.PRO:23:14: Punish him with the rod, and save his soul from Sheol.

evidence.quote: Here begins another series of precepts.

While there is little danger that the use of the "divine
ordinance of the rod" will produce bodily harm, there is great hope of
spiritual good.

primaryText.PRO:23:15: My son, if your heart is wise, then my heart will be glad, even mine.
primaryText.PRO:23:16: Yes, my heart will rejoice when your lips speak what is right.

evidence.quote:
The pleasure afforded the teacher by the pupil's progress is
a motive to diligence.

my reins--(Compare

Ps 7:9).

primaryText.PRO:23:17: Don’t let your heart envy sinners, but rather fear the LORD all day long.
primaryText.PRO:23:18: Indeed surely there is a future hope, and your hope will not be cut off.

evidence.quote: (Compare Margin). The prosperity of the wicked is short.

an end--or, "hereafter," another time, when apparent inequalities
shall be adjusted (compare

Ps 37:28-38).

primaryText.PRO:23:19: Listen, my son, and be wise, and keep your heart on the right path!
primaryText.PRO:23:20: Don’t be among ones drinking too much wine, or those who gorge themselves on meat;
primaryText.PRO:23:21: for the drunkard and the glutton shall become poor; and drowsiness clothes them in rags.

evidence.quote:
guide . . . way--or direct thy thoughts to a right course of
conduct (compare

Pr 4:4; 9:6).

riotous . . . flesh--prodigal, or eating more than necessary.
Instead of "their flesh" (compare Margin), better, "flesh to them,"
that is, used for pleasure.
drowsiness--the dreamy sleep of the slothful.

primaryText.PRO:23:22: Listen to your father who gave you life, and don’t despise your mother when she is old.
primaryText.PRO:23:23: Buy the truth, and don’t sell it. Get wisdom, discipline, and understanding.
primaryText.PRO:23:24: The father of the righteous has great joy. Whoever fathers a wise child delights in him.
primaryText.PRO:23:25: Let your father and your mother be glad! Let her who bore you rejoice!

evidence.quote:
Hearken--that is, obey

(Pr 1:8;
Eph 6:1).

despise . . . old--Adults revere the parents whom, as children, they
once obeyed.

Buy--literally, "get"

(Pr 4:5).

truth--generally and specially as opposed to errors of all kinds.

primaryText.PRO:23:28: Yes, she lies in wait like a robber, and increases the unfaithful among men.

evidence.quote:
A solemn warning against whoredom and drunkenness

(Ho 4:11).

give me--This is the address of that divine wisdom so often presented

(Pr 8:1; 9:3,

&c.).

heart--confidence.

observe--keep.

my ways--such as I teach you

(Pr 3:17; 9:6).

deep ditch--a narrow pit, out of which it is hard to climb.

lieth in wait--to ensnare men into the pit, as hunters entrap game
(compare

Pr 22:14).

increaseth . . . transgressors--

(Pr 5:8-10).

The vice alluded to is peculiarly hardening to the heart.

primaryText.PRO:23:29: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaints? Who has needless bruises? Who has bloodshot eyes?
primaryText.PRO:23:30: Those who stay long at the wine; those who go to seek out mixed wine.

evidence.quote:
A solemn warning against whoredom and drunkenness

(Ho 4:11).

give me--This is the address of that divine wisdom so often presented

(Pr 8:1; 9:3,

&c.).

heart--confidence.

observe--keep.

my ways--such as I teach you

(Pr 3:17; 9:6).

mixed wine--(Compare

Pr 9:2;
Isa 5:11).

evidence.quote:
A solemn warning against whoredom and drunkenness

give me--This is the address of that divine wisdom so often presented

&c.).

heart--confidence.

observe--keep.

my ways--such as I teach you

De 32:14).

giveth . . . cup--literally, "gives its eye," that is, sparkles.

The acute miseries resulting from drunkenness contrasted with the
temptations.

primaryText.PRO:23:33: Your eyes will see strange things, and your mind will imagine confusing things.
primaryText.PRO:23:34: Yes, you will be as he who lies down in the middle of the sea, or as he who lies on top of the rigging:

evidence.quote:
A solemn warning against whoredom and drunkenness

(Ho 4:11).

give me--This is the address of that divine wisdom so often presented

(Pr 8:1; 9:3,

&c.).

heart--confidence.

observe--keep.

my ways--such as I teach you

(Pr 3:17; 9:6).

The moral effects: it inflames passion

(Ge 19:31, 35),

lays open the heart, produces insensibility to the greatest dangers,
and debars from reformation, under the severest sufferings.

evidence.quote:

give me--This is the address of that divine wisdom so often presented

heart--confidence.

observe--keep.

primaryText.PRO:24:2: for their hearts plot violence and their lips talk about mischief.

evidence.quote:
studieth--meditateth.

talk . . . mischief--Their expressed purposes are to do evil.

primaryText.PRO:24:3: Through wisdom a house is built; by understanding it is established;
primaryText.PRO:24:4: by knowledge the rooms are filled with all rare and beautiful treasure.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 14:1;
Isa 54:14).

house--including the family.

by knowledge . . . riches--

(Pr 8:18; 21:20).

primaryText.PRO:24:5: A wise man has great power. A knowledgeable man increases strength,
primaryText.PRO:24:6: for by wise guidance you wage your war, and victory is in many advisors.

evidence.quote:
The general statement

(Ec 9:16, 18)

is specially illustrated (compare

Pr 21:22;
Ps 144:1).

primaryText.PRO:24:7: Wisdom is too high for a fool. He doesn’t open his mouth in the gate.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 14:16).

in the gate--(Compare

Pr 22:22).

primaryText.PRO:24:9: The schemes of folly are sin. The mocker is detested by men.

evidence.quote: So called even if he fails to do evil.
Same thought varied.

primaryText.PRO:24:10: If you falter in the time of trouble, your strength is small.

evidence.quote:
Literally, "If thou fail in the day of straits (adversity),
strait (or, small) is thy strength," which is then truly tested.

primaryText.PRO:24:11: Rescue those who are being led away to death! Indeed, hold back those who are staggering to the slaughter!
primaryText.PRO:24:12: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this,” doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not give to every man according to his work?

evidence.quote:
Neglect of known duty is sin

(Jas 4:17).

ready--literally, "bowing down"

to be slain--that is, unjustly. God's retributive justice cannot be
avoided by professed ignorance.

primaryText.PRO:24:13: My son, eat honey, for it is good, the droppings of the honeycomb, which are sweet to your taste;
primaryText.PRO:24:14: so you shall know wisdom to be to your soul. If you have found it, then there will be a reward: Your hope will not be cut off.

evidence.quote:
As delicious food whets the appetite, so should the rewards of
wisdom excite us to seek it.

primaryText.PRO:24:15: Don’t lay in wait, wicked man, against the habitation of the righteous. Don’t destroy his resting place;
primaryText.PRO:24:16: for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again, but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.

evidence.quote:
The plots of the wicked against the good, though partially,
shall not be fully successful

(Ps 37:24);

while the wicked, falling under penal evil, find no help.

seven times--often, or many

(Pr 6:16, 31; 9:1).

primaryText.PRO:24:17: Don’t rejoice when your enemy falls. Don’t let your heart be glad when he is overthrown,
primaryText.PRO:24:18: lest the LORD see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him.

evidence.quote:
Yet let none rejoice over the fate of evildoers, lest God
punish their wrong spirit by relieving the sufferer (compare

Pr 17:5;
Job 31:29).

primaryText.PRO:24:19: Don’t fret yourself because of evildoers, neither be envious of the wicked;
primaryText.PRO:24:20: for there will be no reward to the evil man. The lamp of the wicked will be snuffed out.

evidence.quote:
candle--or, "prosperity"; it shall come to an end

(Pr 13:9; 20:20).

primaryText.PRO:24:22: for their calamity will rise suddenly. Who knows what destruction may come from them both?

evidence.quote:
A warning against impiety and resistance to lawful rule

(Ro 13:1-7;
1Pe 2:17).

meddle . . . change--(Compare Margin), literally, "mingle not
yourself," avoid the society of restless persons.

their calamity, &c.--either what God and the king inflict, or
what changers and their company suffer; better the first.

primaryText.PRO:24:23: These also are sayings of the wise: To show partiality in judgment is not good.

evidence.quote:
These . . . wise--literally, "are of the wise," as authors
(compare "Psalms of David," Hebrew). "These" refers to the verses
following,

Pr 24:24-34.

to have respect--literally, "to discern faces," show partiality,

primaryText.PRO:24:24: He who says to the wicked, “You are righteous,” peoples will curse him, and nations will abhor him—
primaryText.PRO:24:25: but it will go well with those who convict the guilty, and a rich blessing will come on them.

evidence.quote:
of which an example is justifying the wicked, to which is
opposed, rebuking him, which has a blessing.

(Ps 2:12;
So 8:1).

right answer--literally, "plain words" (compare

Pr 8:9),

opposed to deceptive, or obscure.

primaryText.PRO:24:27: Prepare your work outside, and get your fields ready. Afterwards, build your house.

evidence.quote:
Prepare . . . in the field--Secure, by diligence, a proper support,
and then build; provide necessaries, then comforts, to which a house
rather pertained, in a mild climate, permitting the use of tents.

primaryText.PRO:24:28: Don’t be a witness against your neighbor without cause. Don’t deceive with your lips.
primaryText.PRO:24:29: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work.”

evidence.quote:
Do not speak even truth needlessly against any, and never
falsehood.

primaryText.PRO:24:30: I went by the field of the sluggard, by the vineyard of the man void of understanding.
primaryText.PRO:24:31: Behold, it was all grown over with thorns. Its surface was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.

evidence.quote: A striking picture of the effects of sloth.

primaryText.PRO:24:32: Then I saw, and considered well. I saw, and received instruction:
primaryText.PRO:24:33: a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep,
primaryText.PRO:24:34: so your poverty will come as a robber and your want as an armed man.

evidence.quote:
From the folly of the sluggard learn wisdom

(Pr 6:10, 11).

primaryText.PRO:25:1: These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out.
primaryText.PRO:25:2: It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter.
primaryText.PRO:25:3: As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the hearts of kings are unsearchable.

evidence.quote:
The character of these proverbs sustains the title
(see

Introduction).

also--refers to the former part of the book.

copied out--literally, "transferred," that is, from some other book
to this; not given from memory.

Ye wisely keeping state secrets, which to common men are as
inaccessible heights and depths.

primaryText.PRO:25:4: Take away the dross from the silver, and material comes out for the refiner.
primaryText.PRO:25:5: Take away the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness.

evidence.quote:
As separating impurities from ore leaves pure silver, so taking
from a king wicked counsellors leaves a wise and beneficent government.
before--or, "in presence of," as courtiers stood about a king.

primaryText.PRO:25:6: Don’t exalt yourself in the presence of the king, or claim a place among great men;
primaryText.PRO:25:7: for it is better that it be said to you, “Come up here,” than that you should be put lower in the presence of the prince, whom your eyes have seen.

evidence.quote:
Do not intrude into the presence of the king, for the elevation
of the humble is honorable, but the humbling of the proud disgraceful

(Lu 14:8-10).

primaryText.PRO:25:8: Don’t be hasty in bringing charges to court. What will you do in the end when your neighbor shames you?

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 3:30).

lest . . . shame--lest you do what you ought not, when shamed by
defeat, or "lest thou art shut out from doing any thing."

primaryText.PRO:25:10: lest one who hears it put you to shame, and your bad reputation never depart.
primaryText.PRO:25:9: Debate your case with your neighbor, and don’t betray the confidence of another,

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Mt 5:25,

Margin).

secret--that is, of your opponent, for his disadvantage, and so you
be disgraced, not having discussed your difficulties with him.

primaryText.PRO:25:11: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
primaryText.PRO:25:12: As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover to an obedient ear.

evidence.quote:
a word fitly--literally, "quickly," as wheels roll, just in time.
The comparison as apples . . . silver gives a like sense.

apples, &c.--either real apples of golden color, in a silver network
basket, or imitations on silver embroidery.

Those who desire to know and do rightly, most highly esteem good
counsel

(Pr 9:9; 15:31).

The listening ear is better than one hung with gold.

primaryText.PRO:25:13: As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.

evidence.quote:
Snow from mountains was used to cool drinks; so refreshing is a
faithful messenger

(Pr 13:17).

evidence.quote:
clouds--literally, "vapors"

(Jer 10:13),

clouds only in appearance.

a false gift--promised, but not given.

primaryText.PRO:25:15: By patience a ruler is persuaded. A soft tongue breaks the bone.

evidence.quote:
Gentleness and kindness overcome the most powerful and obstinate.

long forbearing--or, "slowness to anger"

(Pr 14:29; 15:18).

lead your friend to hate you.

primaryText.PRO:25:19: Confidence in someone unfaithful in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a lame foot.
primaryText.PRO:25:20: As one who takes away a garment in cold weather, or vinegar on soda, so is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.

evidence.quote:
A false witness is as destructive to reputation, as such
weapons to the body

(Pr 24:28).

beareth . . . witness--literally, "answereth questions," as before a
judge, against his neighbor.
Treachery annoys as well as deceives.

Not only is the incongruity of songs (that is, joyful) and
sadness meant, but an accession of sadness, by want of sympathy, is
implied.

primaryText.PRO:25:21: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink;
primaryText.PRO:25:22: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and the LORD will reward you.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Mt 5:44;
Ro 12:20).

As metals are melted by heaping coals upon them, so is the heart
softened by kindness.

primaryText.PRO:25:23: The north wind produces rain; so a backbiting tongue brings an angry face.

evidence.quote:
Better, "As the north wind bringeth forth

(Ps 90:2)

or produces rain, so does a concealed or slandering tongue produce
anger."

primaryText.PRO:25:24: It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop than to share a house with a contentious woman.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 21:9, 19).

primaryText.PRO:25:25: Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.
primaryText.PRO:25:26: Like a muddied spring and a polluted well, so is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 25:13).

good news--that is, of some loved interest or absent friend, the more
grateful as coming from afar.

From troubled fountains and corrupt springs no healthy water is to
be had, so when the righteous are oppressed by the wicked, their power
for good is lessened or destroyed.

primaryText.PRO:25:27: It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it honorable to seek one’s own honor.

evidence.quote:
Satiety surfeits

(Pr 25:16);

so men who are self-glorious find shame.

is not glory--"not" is supplied from the first clause, or "is
grievous," in which sense a similar word is used

(Pr 27:2).

primaryText.PRO:25:28: Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man whose spirit is without restraint.

evidence.quote:
Such are exposed to the incursions of evil thoughts and successful
temptations.

primaryText.PRO:26:1: Like snow in summer, and as rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool.
primaryText.PRO:26:2: Like a fluttering sparrow, like a darting swallow, so the undeserved curse doesn’t come to rest.
primaryText.PRO:26:3: A whip is for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools!

evidence.quote:
The incongruities of nature illustrate also those of the moral
world. The fool's unworthiness is also implied

(Pr 17:7; 19:10).

Though not obvious to us,

the bird--literally, "sparrow"--and

swallow--have an object in their motions, so penal evil falls on
none without a reason.

The rod is as much needed by fools and as well suited to them, as
whips and bridles are for beasts.

primaryText.PRO:26:4: Don’t answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also be like him.
primaryText.PRO:26:5: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.

evidence.quote: Answer not--that is, approvingly by like folly.
Answer--by reproof.

primaryText.PRO:26:6: One who sends a message by the hand of a fool is cutting off feet and drinking violence.
primaryText.PRO:26:7: Like the legs of the lame that hang loose, so is a parable in the mouth of fools.
primaryText.PRO:26:8: As one who binds a stone in a sling, so is he who gives honor to a fool.
primaryText.PRO:26:9: Like a thorn bush that goes into the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouth of fools.

evidence.quote:
A fool fails by folly as surely as if he were maimed.

drinketh damage--that is, gets it abundantly

(Job 15:16; 34:7).

legs . . . equal--or, "take away the legs," or "the legs . . . are
weak." In any case the idea is that they are the occasion of an
awkwardness, such as the fool shows in using a parable or proverb
(see

Introduction;

Pr 17:7).

A stone, bound in a sling, is useless; so honor, conferred on a
fool, is thrown away.

As vexatious and unmanageable as a thorn in a drunkard's hand is
a parable to a fool. He will be as apt to misuse is as to use it
rightly.

primaryText.PRO:26:10: As an archer who wounds all, so is he who hires a fool or he who hires those who pass by.
primaryText.PRO:26:11: As a dog that returns to his vomit, so is a fool who repeats his folly.
primaryText.PRO:26:12: Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.

evidence.quote:
Various versions of this are proposed (compare
Margin). Better perhaps--"Much He injures (or literally,
"wounds") all who reward," &c., that is, society is injured by
encouraging evil men.

transgressors--may be rendered "vagrants." The word "God" is improperly
supplied.

returneth . . . folly--Though disgusting to others, the fool
delights in his folly.
The self-conceited are taught with more difficulty than the stupid.

primaryText.PRO:26:13: The sluggard says, “There is a lion in the road! A fierce lion roams the streets!”
primaryText.PRO:26:14: As the door turns on its hinges, so does the sluggard on his bed.
primaryText.PRO:26:15: The sluggard buries his hand in the dish. He is too lazy to bring it back to his mouth.
primaryText.PRO:26:16: The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer with discretion.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 22:13).

(Compare

Pr 6:10; 24:33).

(Compare

Pr 19:24).
The thoughtless being ignorant of their ignorance are conceited.

primaryText.PRO:26:17: Like one who grabs a dog’s ears is one who passes by and meddles in a quarrel not his own.
primaryText.PRO:26:18: Like a madman who shoots torches, arrows, and death,
primaryText.PRO:26:19: is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, “Am I not joking?”

evidence.quote:
meddleth--as in

Pr 20:19; 24:21;

as either holding a dog by the ears or letting him go involves danger,
so success in another man's strife or failure involves a useless risk
of reputation, does no good, and may do us harm.
Such are reckless of results.

primaryText.PRO:26:20: For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.
primaryText.PRO:26:21: As coals are to hot embers, and wood to fire, so is a contentious man to kindling strife.
primaryText.PRO:26:22: The words of a whisperer are as dainty morsels, they go down into the innermost parts.

evidence.quote:
The talebearers foster

(Pr 16:28),

and the contentious excite, strife.

(Compare

Pr 18:8).

primaryText.PRO:26:23: Like silver dross on an earthen vessel are the lips of a fervent one with an evil heart.
primaryText.PRO:26:24: A malicious man disguises himself with his lips, but he harbors evil in his heart.
primaryText.PRO:26:25: When his speech is charming, don’t believe him, for there are seven abominations in his heart.
primaryText.PRO:26:26: His malice may be concealed by deception, but his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.

evidence.quote:
Warm professions can no more give value to insincerity than
silver coating to rude earthenware.

dissembleth--though an unusual sense of the word (compare
Margin), is allowable, and better suits the context, which sets
forth hypocrisy.

Sentiment of

Pr 26:24

carried out.

seven abominations in his heart--that is, very many (compare

Pr 24:16).

Deceit will at last be exposed, and the wicked by their own
arts often bring on retribution (compare

Pr 12:13;
Ps 7:16; 9:17,

&c.).

primaryText.PRO:26:27: Whoever digs a pit shall fall into it. Whoever rolls a stone, it will come back on him.
primaryText.PRO:26:28: A lying tongue hates those it hurts; and a flattering mouth works ruin.

evidence.quote:
Deceit will at last be exposed, and the wicked by their own
arts often bring on retribution (compare

Pr 12:13;
Ps 7:16; 9:17,

&c.).

Men hate those they injure.

A lying tongue--"lips" for the persons (compare

Pr 4:24;
Ps 12:3).

primaryText.PRO:27:1: Don’t boast about tomorrow; for you don’t know what a day may bring.
primaryText.PRO:27:2: Let another man praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips.

evidence.quote: Avoid self-praise.

primaryText.PRO:27:3: A stone is heavy, and sand is a burden; but a fool’s provocation is heavier than both.
primaryText.PRO:27:4: Wrath is cruel, and anger is overwhelming; but who is able to stand before jealousy?

evidence.quote:
heavy--The literal sense of "heavy," applied to material subjects,
illustrates its figurative, "grievous," applied to moral.

a fool's wrath--is unreasonable and excessive.

primaryText.PRO:27:5: Better is open rebuke than hidden love.
primaryText.PRO:27:6: The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.

evidence.quote:
secret love--not manifested in acts is useless; and even, if
its exhibition by rebukes wounds us, such love is preferable to the
frequent (compare Margin), and hence deceitful, kisses of an enemy.

primaryText.PRO:27:7: A full soul loathes a honeycomb; but to a hungry soul, every bitter thing is sweet.
primaryText.PRO:27:8: As a bird that wanders from her nest, so is a man who wanders from his home.

evidence.quote:
The luxury of wealth confers less happiness than the healthy
appetite of labor.
Such are not only out of place, but out of duty and in danger.

primaryText.PRO:27:10: Don’t forsake your friend and your father’s friend. Don’t go to your brother’s house in the day of your disaster. A neighbor who is near is better than a distant brother.
primaryText.PRO:27:9: Perfume and incense bring joy to the heart; so does earnest counsel from a man’s friend.

evidence.quote:
rejoice the heart--the organ of perceiving what pleases the senses.

sweetness . . . counsel--or, "wise counsel is also pleasing."

Adhere to tried friends. The ties of blood may be less reliable
than those of genuine friendship.

primaryText.PRO:27:11: Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, then I can answer my tormentor.
primaryText.PRO:27:12: A prudent man sees danger and takes refuge; but the simple pass on, and suffer for it.
primaryText.PRO:27:13: Take his garment when he puts up collateral for a stranger. Hold it for a wayward woman!

evidence.quote:
The wisdom of children both reflects credit on parents and
contributes to their aid in difficulties.

(Compare

Pr 20:16; 22:3).

primaryText.PRO:27:14: He who blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning, it will be taken as a curse by him.
primaryText.PRO:27:15: A continual dropping on a rainy day and a contentious wife are alike:
primaryText.PRO:27:16: restraining her is like restraining the wind, or like grasping oil in his right hand.

evidence.quote: Excessive zeal in praising raises suspicions of selfishness.

(Compare

Pr 19:13).

very . . . day--literally, "a day of showers."

hideth--or, "restrains" (that is, tries to do it); is as fruitless
an effort, as that of holding the wind.

the ointment of his right hand--the organ of power

(Ps 17:7; 18:35).

His right hand endeavors to repress perfume, but vainly. Some prefer:
"His right hand comes on oil," that is, "cannot take hold." Such a
woman cannot be tamed.

primaryText.PRO:27:17: Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.
primaryText.PRO:27:18: Whoever tends the fig tree shall eat its fruit. He who looks after his master shall be honored.
primaryText.PRO:27:19: Like water reflects a face, so a man’s heart reflects the man.

evidence.quote:
a man sharpeneth . . . friend--that is, conversation promotes
intelligence, which the face exhibits.
Diligence secures a reward, even for the humble servant.
We may see our characters in the developed tempers of others.

primaryText.PRO:27:20: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; and a man’s eyes are never satisfied.
primaryText.PRO:27:21: The crucible is for silver, and the furnace for gold; but man is refined by his praise.
primaryText.PRO:27:22: Though you grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with grain, yet his foolishness will not be removed from him.

evidence.quote: Men's cupidity is as insatiable as the grave.

Praise tests character.

a man to his praise--according to his praise, as he bears it. Thus
vain men seek it, weak men are inflated by it, wise men disregard it,
&c.

The obstinate wickedness of such is incurable by the heaviest
inflictions.

primaryText.PRO:27:23: Know well the state of your flocks, and pay attention to your herds,
primaryText.PRO:27:24: for riches are not forever, nor does the crown endure to all generations.
primaryText.PRO:27:25: The hay is removed, and the new growth appears, the grasses of the hills are gathered in.
primaryText.PRO:27:26: The lambs are for your clothing, and the goats are the price of a field.
primaryText.PRO:27:27: There will be plenty of goats’ milk for your food, for your family’s food, and for the nourishment of your servant girls.

evidence.quote:
flocks--constituted the staple of wealth. It is only by care
and diligence that the most solid possessions can be perpetuated

(Pr 23:5).

The fact that providential arrangements furnish the means of
competence to those who properly use them is another motive to diligence
(compare

Ps 65:9-13).

The hay appeareth--literally, "Grass appeareth"

(Job 40:15;
Ps 104:14).

primaryText.PRO:28:1: The wicked flee when no one pursues; but the righteous are as bold as a lion.
primaryText.PRO:28:2: In rebellion, a land has many rulers, but order is maintained by a man of understanding and knowledge.
primaryText.PRO:28:3: A needy man who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain which leaves no crops.

evidence.quote:
Anarchy producing contending rulers shortens the reign of each.

but by a man . . . prolonged--or, "by a man of understanding--that
is, a good ruler--he who knows or regards the right, that is, a good
citizen, shall prolong (his days)." Good rulers are a blessing to the
people. Bad government as a punishment for evil is contrasted with good
as blessing to the good.

A poor man, &c.--Such, in power, exact more severely, and so leave
subjects bare.

primaryText.PRO:28:4: Those who forsake the law praise the wicked; but those who keep the law contend with them.
primaryText.PRO:28:5: Evil men don’t understand justice; but those who seek the LORD understand it fully.
primaryText.PRO:28:6: Better is the poor who walks in his integrity than he who is perverse in his ways, and he is rich.

evidence.quote: They that forsake . . . wicked--Wrongdoers encourage one another.

(Compare

Joh 7:17).

Ignorance of moral truth is due to unwillingness to know it.

(Compare

Pr 10:6).

Riches cannot compensate for sin, nor the want of them affect
integrity.

primaryText.PRO:28:7: Whoever keeps the law is a wise son; but he who is a companion of gluttons shames his father.
primaryText.PRO:28:8: He who increases his wealth by excessive interest gathers it for one who has pity on the poor.
primaryText.PRO:28:9: He who turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 17:25).

riotous men--or, "gluttons"

(Pr 23:20, 21).

usury . . . unjust gain--(Compare Margin). The two terms,
meaning nearly the same, may denote excessive interest. God's providence
directs the proper use of wealth.

(Compare

Pr 15:8; 21:27).

hearing--that is, obeying. God requires sincere worshippers

(Ps 66:18;
Joh 4:24).

primaryText.PRO:28:10: Whoever causes the upright to go astray in an evil way, he will fall into his own trap; but the blameless will inherit good.
primaryText.PRO:28:11: The rich man is wise in his own eyes; but the poor who has understanding sees through him.
primaryText.PRO:28:12: When the righteous triumph, there is great glory; but when the wicked rise, men hide themselves.
primaryText.PRO:28:13: He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 26:27).

A poor but wise man can discover (and expose) the rich and
self-conceited.

great glory--or, cause for it to a people, for the righteous
rejoice in good, and righteousness exalts a nation

(Pr 14:34).

a man . . . hidden--that is, the good retire, or all kinds try to
escape a wicked rule.

(Compare

Ps 32:3-5).

Concealment of sin delivers none from God's wrath, but He shows mercy
to the humble penitent

(Ps 51:4).

primaryText.PRO:28:14: Blessed is the man who always fears; but one who hardens his heart falls into trouble.
primaryText.PRO:28:15: As a roaring lion or a charging bear, so is a wicked ruler over helpless people.
primaryText.PRO:28:16: A tyrannical ruler lacks judgment. One who hates ill-gotten gain will have long days.
primaryText.PRO:28:17: A man who is tormented by blood guilt will be a fugitive until death. No one will support him.

evidence.quote:
feareth--that is, God, and so repents.

hardeneth his heart--makes himself insensible to sin, and so will not
repent

(Pr 14:16; 29:1).

The rapacity and cruelty of such beasts well represent some wicked
men (compare

Ps 7:2; 17:12).

The prince . . . understanding--that is, He does not perceive
that oppression jeopards his success. Covetousness often produces
oppression, hence the contrast.

doeth violence . . . blood, &c.--or, that is oppressed by the
blood of life

(Ge 9:6),

which he has taken.

to the pit--the grave or destruction

(Pr 1:12;
Job 33:18-24;
Ps 143:7).

stay him--sustain or deliver him.

primaryText.PRO:28:18: Whoever walks blamelessly is kept safe; but one with perverse ways will fall suddenly.
primaryText.PRO:28:19: One who works his land will have an abundance of food; but one who chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.
primaryText.PRO:28:20: A faithful man is rich with blessings; but one who is eager to be rich will not go unpunished.
primaryText.PRO:28:21: To show partiality is not good, yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 10:9; 17:20).

Double dealing is eventually fatal.

(Compare

Pr 10:4; 20:4).

vain persons--idle, useless drones, implying that they are also wicked

(Pr 12:11;
Ps 26:4).

maketh haste . . . rich--implying
deceit or fraud

(Pr 20:21),

and so opposed to "faithful" or reliable.

respect of persons--

(Pr 24:23).

Such are led to evil by the slightest motive.

primaryText.PRO:28:22: A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him.
primaryText.PRO:28:23: One who rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than one who flatters with the tongue.
primaryText.PRO:28:24: Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, “It’s not wrong,” is a partner with a destroyer.
primaryText.PRO:28:25: One who is greedy stirs up strife; but one who trusts in the LORD will prosper.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 28:20).

evil eye--in the general sense of

Pr 23:6,

here more specific for covetousness (compare

Pr 22:9;
Mt 20:15).

poverty . . . him--by God's providence.

(Compare

Pr 9:8, 9; 27:5).

Those benefited by reproof will love their monitors.

(Compare

Mt 15:4-6).

Such, though heirs, are virtually thieves, to be ranked with
highwaymen.

of a proud heart--literally, "puffed up of soul"--that is,
self-confident, and hence overbearing and litigious.

made fat--or, "prosperous"

(Pr 11:25; 16:20).

primaryText.PRO:28:26: One who trusts in himself is a fool; but one who walks in wisdom is kept safe.
primaryText.PRO:28:27: One who gives to the poor has no lack; but one who closes his eyes will have many curses.
primaryText.PRO:28:28: When the wicked rise, men hide themselves; but when they perish, the righteous thrive.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 3:6-8).

walketh wisely--that is, trusting in God

(Pr 22:17-19).

(Compare

Pr 11:24-26).

hideth his eyes--as the face

(Ps 27:9; 69:17),

denotes inattention.

The elevation of the wicked to power drives men to seek refuge from
tyranny (compare

Pr 28:12; 11:10;
Ps 12:8).

primaryText.PRO:29:1: He who is often rebuked and stiffens his neck will be destroyed suddenly, with no remedy.
primaryText.PRO:29:2: When the righteous thrive, the people rejoice; but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
primaryText.PRO:29:3: Whoever loves wisdom brings joy to his father; but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.
primaryText.PRO:29:4: The king by justice makes the land stable, but he who takes bribes tears it down.

evidence.quote:
hardeneth . . . neck--obstinately refuses counsel

(2Ki 17:14;
Ne 9:16).

destroyed--literally, "shivered" or "utterly broken to pieces."

without remedy--literally, "without healing" or repairing.

(Compare

Pr 11:10; 28:28).

in authority--(Compare Margin), increased in power.

by judgment--that is, righteous decisions, opposed to those
procured by gifts (compare

Pr 28:21),

by which good government is perverted.

land--for nation.

primaryText.PRO:29:5: A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.
primaryText.PRO:29:6: An evil man is snared by his sin, but the righteous can sing and be glad.
primaryText.PRO:29:7: The righteous care about justice for the poor. The wicked aren’t concerned about knowledge.
primaryText.PRO:29:8: Mockers stir up a city, but wise men turn away anger.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 26:28).

spreadeth . . . feet--By misleading him as to his real character, the
flatterer brings him to evil, prepared by himself or others.

In--or, "By"

the transgression--he is brought into difficulty

(Pr 12:13),

but the righteous go on prospering, and so sing or rejoice.

considereth--literally, "knows," as

Ps 1:6.

the cause--that is, in courts of justice (compare

Pr 29:14).

The voluntary neglect of it by the wicked

(Pr 28:27)

occasions oppression.

Scornful men--those who contemptuously disregard God's law.

bring--(Compare Margin), kindle strife.

turn away wrath--that is, "abate wrath."

primaryText.PRO:29:10: The bloodthirsty hate a man of integrity; and they seek the life of the upright.
primaryText.PRO:29:11: A fool vents all of his anger, but a wise man brings himself under control.
primaryText.PRO:29:12: If a ruler listens to lies, all of his officials are wicked.
primaryText.PRO:29:9: If a wise man goes to court with a foolish man, the fool rages or scoffs, and there is no peace.

evidence.quote:
contendeth--that is, in law.

whether . . . laugh--The fool, whether angry or good-humored, is
unsettled; or referring the words to the wise man, the sense is, that
all his efforts, severe or gentle, are unavailing to pacify the fool.

bloodthirsty--(Compare Margin), murderers

(Ps 5:6; 26:9).

hate, &c.--

(Pr 1:11;
Ge 3:4).

seek . . . soul--that is, to preserve it.

(Compare

Pr 12:16; 16:32).

mind--or, "spirit," for anger or any ill passion which the righteous
restrain.
His servants imitate him.

primaryText.PRO:29:13: The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives sight to the eyes of both.
primaryText.PRO:29:14: The king who fairly judges the poor, his throne shall be established forever.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 22:2).

deceitful man--literally, "man of vexations," an exactor.

the Lord . . . their eyes--sustains their lives

(1Sa 14:27;
Ps 13:3);

that is, both depend on Him, and He will do justice.

(Compare

Pr 20:28; 25:5).

Such is the character of the King of kings

(Ps 72:4, 12).

primaryText.PRO:29:15: The rod of correction gives wisdom, but a child left to himself causes shame to his mother.
primaryText.PRO:29:16: When the wicked increase, sin increases; but the righteous will see their downfall.
primaryText.PRO:29:17: Correct your son, and he will give you peace; yes, he will bring delight to your soul.
primaryText.PRO:29:18: Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint; but one who keeps the law is blessed.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 29:2, 12;
Ps 12:1-8).

shall see . . . fall--and triumph in it

(Ps 37:34-38; 58:10, 11).

(Compare

Pr 29:3, 15;
Pr 19:18).

give thee rest--peace and quiet (compare

Pr 29:9).

no vision--instruction in God's truth, which was by prophets,
through visions

(1Sa 3:1).

people perish--(Compare Margin), are deprived of moral restraints.

keepeth the law--has, and observes, instruction

(Pr 14:11, 34;
Ps 19:11).

primaryText.PRO:29:19: A servant can’t be corrected by words. Though he understands, yet he will not respond.

evidence.quote:
A servant--who lacks good principle.

corrected--or discovered.

will not answer--that is, will not obey.

primaryText.PRO:29:20: Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
primaryText.PRO:29:21: He who pampers his servant from youth will have him become a son in the end.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 21:5).

hasty in . . . words?--implying self-conceit

(Pr 26:12).
become his son--assume the place and privileges of one.

primaryText.PRO:29:22: An angry man stirs up strife, and a wrathful man abounds in sin.
primaryText.PRO:29:23: A man’s pride brings him low, but one of lowly spirit gains honor.
primaryText.PRO:29:24: Whoever is an accomplice of a thief is an enemy of his own soul. He takes an oath, but dares not testify.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 15:18).

Such are delighted by discord and violence.

(Compare

Pr 16:18; 18:12).

honour . . . spirit--or, "such shall lay hold on honor"

(Pr 11:16).

hateth . . . soul--(Compare

Pr 8:36).

heareth cursing--

(Le 5:1),

risks the punishment, rather than reveal truth.

primaryText.PRO:29:25: The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in the LORD is kept safe.
primaryText.PRO:29:26: Many seek the ruler’s favor, but a man’s justice comes from the LORD.

evidence.quote:
The fear . . . snare--involves men in difficulty (compare

Pr 29:6).

shall be safe--(Compare Margin;

Pr 18:10).

primaryText.PRO:29:27: A dishonest man detests the righteous, and the upright in their ways detest the wicked.

evidence.quote:
(Compare

Pr 3:32).

On last clause, compare

Pr 29:16;
Ps 37:12.

primaryText.PRO:30:1: The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, the revelation: the man says to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:

evidence.quote:
This is the title of this chapter
(see

Introduction).

the prophecy--literally, "the burden" (compare

Isa 13:1;
Zec 9:1),

used for any divine instruction; not necessarily a prediction, which was
only a kind of prophecy

(1Ch 15:27,

"a song"). Prophets were inspired men, who spoke for God to man, or for
man to God

(Ge 20:7;
Ex 7:14, 15, 16).

Such, also, were the New Testament prophets. In a general sense, Gad,
Nathan, and others were such, who were divine teachers, though we do
not learn that they ever predicted.

the man spake--literally, "the saying of the man"; an expression used
to denote any solemn and important announcement (compare

2Sa 23:1;
Ps 36:1; 110:1;
Isa 1:24,

&c.). Ithiel and Ucal were perhaps pupils.

primaryText.PRO:30:2: “Surely I am the most ignorant man, and don’t have a man’s understanding.
primaryText.PRO:30:3: I have not learned wisdom, neither do I have the knowledge of the Holy One.
primaryText.PRO:30:4: Who has ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has bound the waters in his garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son’s name, if you know?

evidence.quote:
brutish--stupid, a strong term to denote his lowly
self-estimation; or he may speak of such as his natural condition, as
contrasted with God's all-seeing comprehensive knowledge and almighty
power. The questions of this clause emphatically deny the attributes
